title: Aged Care Support Systems
oneLine: Give older people more control over everyday support, while making the work of care teams easier.
need: A missed handover, confusing appointment or hard-to-reach light switch can make an ordinary day unnecessarily difficult. Start with older people describing the parts of home life they want to keep doing for themselves. Family expectations, staff workload and the person's own wishes may differ; the service must make those differences discussable.
offer: Explore a support service combining accessible reminders, simple environmental controls and a clear human handover. The first product could be a well-designed coordination tool rather than a robot. Women who have delivered years of paid or unpaid care would shape the product and hold decision-making roles, with accessibility built into procurement and support.
users: Older people directing their own support
Family members invited by the person

firstPilot.title: One everyday routine, designed together
steps: Invite a willing care group to map a routine such as preparing for an outing, including the person's own choices.
Prototype the reminder and handover with paper screens and existing accessible devices before collecting sensitive information.
Try the workflow with consenting adults, a named support person and a clear way to stop the trial.
Compare missed steps, time spent coordinating and whether participants feel more independent.
firstPilot.deliverable: An accessible service walkthrough, a tested handover template and a short account of what participants would change.

evidence.known: The planning document places care and useful AI alongside women's executive development. It does not identify a functioning care product.
evidence.unknown: Whether the proposed workflow helps people without increasing supervision, alerts or dependence on technology.
evidence.nextMeasurement: User-rated control over the routine, completed handovers and coordinator time against the previous process.

businessModel: Explore a service agreement with a care provider or a supported household, priced around setup, training and ongoing help. Test willingness to pay separately from need.
leadershipDecision: The founder must decide which tasks technology may assist and which decisions remain with the person and qualified care staff.
risks: An alert could be mistaken for a guarantee of safety.
Family convenience could override the older person's choice.
Sensitive household information could be shared too broadly.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Which everyday routines do older women want to control themselves, and where do they want human help?
Would clearer handovers reduce unpaid coordination for carers without overriding the older person's choices?

title: NDIS Support Systems
oneLine: Build disability support around a person's goals, access needs and authority over their own life.
need: Support often crosses providers, appointments, equipment and everyday relationships. People may repeatedly explain what helps them, while small communication failures create large barriers. This concept begins with the participant's chosen activity and preferred communication, including people whose needs are not obvious to an observer.
offer: Develop an accessible planning and coordination service that makes agreements, support preferences and next actions easy to understand. The first version could be a participant-controlled support passport and a practical task board. Any later AI assistant would help prepare and organise information, with human responsibility clearly assigned and participant permission governing sharing.
users: People with disability and their chosen supporters
Support workers learning an agreed routine

firstPilot.title: A participant-owned activity plan
steps: Pay a small disability-led advisory group to choose one recurring activity that needs better coordination.
Co-design the plan in plain language, screen-reader-friendly text and other formats the participants actually use.
Rehearse a handover between two supporters with fictional information before any live use.
Review whether the participant can change permissions, correct the plan and complete the activity with less repeated explanation.
firstPilot.deliverable: A tested accessible plan, permission map and service specification shaped by participants.

evidence.known: The source catalogue names NDIS Support Systems as an enterprise theme; it does not establish eligibility, funding approval or a registered provider.
evidence.unknown: Which coordination task creates enough benefit to justify an additional tool and its ongoing support.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Participant-defined goal progress, repeated explanations avoided and accessibility problems left unresolved.

resources: Current professional advice on the intended service
businessModel: A provider service or participant-selected support product could be explored after its actual funding and purchasing route is checked. Do not assume an expense is claimable.
leadershipDecision: Give participants real authority over product priorities, data access and the definition of a successful outcome.
risks: A rigid workflow could reduce individual choice.
Accessibility could be treated as an optional add-on.
Provider priorities could displace participant goals.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Can a disabled woman choose her goals, communication format and who sees her support preferences?
Would the tool work with changing support workers, limited connectivity and little time to repeat her story?

title: Smart City Capsule Hotels
oneLine: Explore compact city accommodation that makes short stays dignified, accessible and easy to run.
need: Shift workers, learners and travellers may need a reliable short stay without the cost or complexity of a full hotel room. Compact accommodation also raises serious questions about privacy, ventilation, noise, luggage, carers and body size. A glamorous rendering cannot answer whether a real person would sleep comfortably there.
offer: Develop a service and layout study for a small accommodation operator, comparing compact private rooms with capsule arrangements and conventional alternatives. Design with people of different heights, weights and mobility needs. A useful enterprise may emerge from booking, cleaning or guest-support improvements before any purpose-built accommodation is justified.

firstPilot.title: A room you can actually assess
steps: Interview guests about a specific overnight need, including storage, changing clothes, privacy and accessible support.
Build a full-size non-habitable mock-up using temporary partitions and adjustable furniture.
Ask diverse adults to test entry, turning, reaching storage and calling for assistance.
Compare the layout and operating plan with an existing room format, including cleaning time and staff access.
firstPilot.deliverable: A guest-tested layout and operating brief with unresolved building and access requirements clearly listed.

evidence.known: The planning archive proposes capsule hotels; no approved property, operator or compliant design is supplied.
evidence.unknown: Whether space savings remain worthwhile after safe access, ventilation, cleaning and guest comfort are fully costed.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Task completion in the mock-up, comfort feedback and staff minutes required between stays.

businessModel: Test a design and operations service with an existing operator before considering ownership of a property. Revenue assumptions should use that operator's verified demand and costs.
leadershipDecision: Choose the minimum standard of dignity and access the venture will protect even when it reduces room count.
risks: Very small spaces may exclude larger bodies or mobility aids.
Staffing and maintenance costs may erase apparent savings.
Simulation cannot establish building compliance.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Would women of different heights, bust sizes and mobility needs have enough room to sleep, dress and manage luggage?
What privacy, access and staff availability would a woman need when arriving after a late shift?

title: Smart City Quarantine Hotels
oneLine: Design adaptable accommodation workflows for public-health disruptions and supported isolation.
need: During a health disruption, accommodation can become part of a wider response involving guests, staff, transport, clinical advice and public authorities. The historical quarantine-hotel title points to continuity planning, but a current venture should begin with the needs of a willing operator and qualified health advisers rather than assuming another emergency programme.
offer: Explore a planning service for accommodation that can adapt to changing occupancy and separation needs. It could document staff routes, delivery handovers, guest communication and room turnaround, using a simulation to expose conflicts. Clinical decisions, infection-control requirements and any restrictions on movement belong to the responsible authorities and professionals.
users: Guests with access or care requirements

firstPilot.title: A tabletop accommodation exercise
steps: Choose a fictional disruption scenario with a hotel manager and qualified infection-control adviser.
Map clean supplies, waste, meals, staff movement and guest support without using real patient data.
Run the scenario with staff and accessible guest personas, recording conflicting instructions and bottlenecks.
Revise the playbook and identify which changes require engineering assessment or formal authorisation.
firstPilot.deliverable: A reviewed exercise report, operational route map and list of actions for the accommodation operator.

evidence.known: The archive records a quarantine-hotel idea from its original period. It is not evidence of a current public-health contract or clinical service.
evidence.unknown: Whether the operator needs a standalone service or whether existing emergency planning already covers the problem.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Unresolved handover conflicts, time to locate the responsible person and successful completion of the exercise.

businessModel: A preparedness workshop and periodically reviewed operations manual could be a paid business service if an operator identifies a gap.
leadershipDecision: Define the limits of the service so its communications support professional instructions without creating competing medical advice.
risks: A plan could create false confidence if never rehearsed.
Guest dignity may be lost in rigid procedures.
Building constraints may require more than an operational workaround.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: How would women in supported isolation retain privacy, clear information and a meaningful way to raise concerns?
Does the accommodation workflow account for pregnancy, disability, care responsibilities and the people doing room turnaround?

title: Automated Fleet Cleaning
oneLine: Turn fleet cleaning into a measurable service for workers, vehicles and water use.
need: A fleet's cleaning needs vary with vehicle shape, passenger use, salt exposure and operating hours. Repetitive cleaning may be physically demanding, while poorly planned turnaround can leave vehicles unavailable. The opportunity is to understand the actual depot workflow before specifying a robot or automated wash installation.
offer: Develop a cleaning assessment and assisted workflow for one fleet type. Compare existing manual methods, ergonomic equipment and limited automation for a repeatable task such as floor cleaning or exterior rinsing. The venture would document what was cleaned, what still needs human attention and where water or consumables go.

firstPilot.title: One vehicle, one repeatable cleaning task
steps: Observe a consenting crew clean a representative vehicle and record task times, awkward reaches and missed areas.
Agree a cleanliness inspection method with the operator, including surfaces that need specialist treatment.
Trial an existing assisted tool on a non-operational vehicle under controlled conditions.
Compare inspection results, worker effort, water use and total turnaround including setup and pack-down.
firstPilot.deliverable: A measured workflow and equipment decision with worker feedback and a realistic service specification.

evidence.known: The source suggests automated fleet cleaning. It does not nominate a fleet, robot supplier or verified performance target.
evidence.unknown: Whether automation improves the complete shift rather than making one isolated demonstration look faster.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Accepted vehicles per shift, rework rate, water used and worker-reported physical effort.

businessModel: Explore a per-vehicle cleaning service or a depot improvement contract. Include training, downtime, consumables and equipment upkeep in the price.
leadershipDecision: Decide how efficiency gains will improve jobs, pay or service capacity, with the cleaning team involved in that decision.
risks: A machine may miss irregular interior surfaces.
Runoff could require treatment or different handling.
Poor scheduling could shift unpaid work onto cleaners.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Can women doing the cleaning define a better shift, including physical effort, paid time and predictable hours?
Would the tools fit different reaches and body sizes, with a route into technical and supervisory roles?

title: Frozen Food Warehouse Systems
oneLine: Help cold stores keep food traceable, accessible and moving through the right temperature conditions.
need: Frozen warehouses combine stock decisions, loading, staff exposure, packaging and refrigeration demand. A misplaced pallet or slow handover can waste time and put food quality at risk. The first opportunity is often a clearer workflow with trustworthy measurements, rather than a large robotic installation.
offer: Explore a warehouse planning tool that connects stock location, handling steps and energy use. Start with one product family and compare a digital pick plan with current practice. Any sensing or automation should support the operator's food-safety system, with alarms owned by a named person and manual fallback available.

firstPilot.title: Follow one pallet through the cold chain
steps: Map arrival, storage, picking and dispatch for a representative frozen product with the operator.
Create a small digital model using fictional orders or properly authorised operational records.
Test alternative pick sequences without changing live temperature controls or food-handling rules.
Review travel time, stock errors, door openings and how exceptions are communicated between shifts.
firstPilot.deliverable: A baseline workflow, tested pick-planning prototype and a prioritised improvement brief.

evidence.known: The catalogue names frozen-food warehouse systems. The supplied plan supports measuring workload and benefits before purchasing infrastructure.
evidence.unknown: Whether the main constraint is information, physical layout, staffing or refrigeration capacity.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Order accuracy, staff travel distance, exception response time and energy per comparable throughput.

businessModel: Offer a workflow study and supported planning tool, with future automation justified by measured savings and service reliability.
leadershipDecision: Choose which performance measures matter together so faster throughput does not hide damaged stock or harder working conditions.
risks: Incomplete data can produce misleading pick routes.
Overcomplicated alerts can distract staff.
A successful software trial does not validate refrigeration engineering.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Can women move and inspect stock without equipment or protective clothing assuming a single body size?
Who controls shift timing and alerts, and would the system reduce pressure rather than simply demand faster work?

title: Space Port Island Construction
oneLine: Test the assumptions behind an island spaceport before proposing a site or construction programme.
need: The spaceport idea combines launch logistics, coastal engineering, transport, community priorities and environmental consequences. These are substantial dependencies, not details to fill in after choosing an attractive island. The useful starting question is whether any clearly defined mission needs new infrastructure at all.
offer: Create a comparative mission-and-infrastructure study using fictional or publicly documented site characteristics. Explore launch frequency, transport connections, weather exposure, exclusion requirements and maintenance access alongside existing spaceport services. An early enterprise could provide transparent planning models, without representing any island as available or a community as supportive.

firstPilot.title: A no-site-commitment feasibility comparison
steps: Define a representative payload and service need, including why current launch options are insufficient.
Compare existing launch access, a mainland service model and a hypothetical island model using documented assumptions.
Map environmental, aviation, maritime, land and community decision points for each option.
Ask independent specialists to identify missing evidence and the conditions under which the island option should be rejected.
firstPilot.deliverable: A comparison model, dependency map and research brief showing whether further study is warranted.

evidence.known: The archive proposes island spaceport construction. It supplies no selected site, access rights, approvals or engineering feasibility result.
evidence.unknown: Whether island infrastructure offers a defensible advantage once logistics, impacts and operating obligations are included.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Sensitivity of the proposed advantage to launch demand, transport delays and construction or maintenance assumptions.

businessModel: A planning and simulation service is a possible near-term business. Building or operating a spaceport would require a separate case and substantial authorised partners.
leadershipDecision: Require an evidence-based stop decision when an existing service better meets the mission or a community does not want the proposal.
risks: Site imagery may be mistaken for an approved project.
Demand assumptions can dominate the business case.
Coastal exposure can greatly complicate long-term upkeep.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Which women in the affected coastal community would help define the infrastructure question before anyone selects a site?
Would technical jobs and ownership be accessible to local women, and who could challenge the project's claimed benefits?

title: East Coast Under Ocean UFRT
oneLine: Examine whether an under-ocean fast-transport vision has a useful, testable starting point.
need: The original East Coast Under Ocean UFRT title is a large transport vision with many unresolved choices. Routes, vehicle technology, pressure conditions, evacuation, energy supply and demand all need definition. A responsible founder begins with the journey people need, not an assumed tunnel solution.
offer: Develop a comparison of a clearly specified coastal passenger or freight journey against existing transport and proposed alternatives. Preserve UFRT as the archive's label while documenting its intended meaning before engineering analysis. A digital study could expose which assumptions make an under-ocean system attractive and which make it impractical.

firstPilot.title: One journey, competing transport options
steps: Select a journey problem using public demand information and identify who experiences its current limitations.
Specify the proposed operating concept, including speed, stops, capacity and a plain description of the UFRT label.
Compare the concept with improved rail, ferry, road or logistics coordination using consistent assumptions.
Build a failure and evacuation scenario with qualified infrastructure specialists before advancing any route.
firstPilot.deliverable: A transport options brief with a transparent model and explicit unresolved engineering questions.

evidence.known: The source provides the title, not a demonstrated under-ocean system or a surveyed route.
evidence.unknown: Whether the proposed travel benefit survives whole-life cost, geotechnical uncertainty, evacuation and energy requirements.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Door-to-door time, capacity and service continuity across conservative scenarios rather than headline vehicle speed.

businessModel: Early revenue could come from useful transport modelling or journey analysis. A megaproject funding claim would be premature.
leadershipDecision: Choose the transport problem and comparison criteria before investing in a favoured technology or route.
risks: Tunnel and seabed conditions remain highly site-specific.
Emergency access could dominate the design.
Optimistic demand may hide cheaper improvements.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: What would make the complete coastal journey useful for women travelling with children, mobility aids or work equipment?
Could women affected by a proposed route influence access, affordability and emergency arrangements before the technology is chosen?

title: Cinematic Universe Simulations
oneLine: Use shared fictional worlds to explore real choices about future lives, communities and technology.
need: Long-term systems can be hard to discuss through technical reports alone. A simulated story world lets people experience trade-offs, notice missing viewpoints and imagine a life worth building. The challenge is to keep the story emotionally compelling while making its assumptions and invented elements visible.
offer: Create a small playable or cinematic scene in which characters face a practical future dilemma, such as sharing energy or caring for an isolated neighbour. Women of different ages, bodies, skills and styles should hold meaningful roles in the world. A companion discussion guide would connect the experience to a real decision without presenting fiction as a forecast.

firstPilot.title: One scene, one meaningful choice
steps: Choose a decision with a clear human consequence and write the perspectives of several affected characters.
Build a short storyboard or interactive scene using assets the team owns or has permission to use.
Invite a varied audience to play or watch, then discuss whose choices felt absent or constrained.
Revise the scene and publish an assumptions note separating observed facts from authored possibilities.
firstPilot.deliverable: A short experience, audience feedback and a facilitator guide that can support a real discussion.

evidence.known: The plan connects major storytelling with leadership development and the Grain by Grain future-resilience vision.
evidence.unknown: Whether the chosen scene improves understanding or merely reinforces the creators' existing assumptions.
evidence.nextMeasurement: What participants can explain afterwards, which perspectives they identify and the quality of the discussion generated.

resources: Paid performers or voice talent where used
businessModel: Explore commissioned learning experiences, licensing to educators or a production service. Test the audience and distribution route before building a large universe.
leadershipDecision: Decide who has authorship, payment, credit and the ability to challenge how their community is represented.
risks: A beautiful world may disguise weak assumptions.
Interactive choices can oversimplify political trade-offs.
Generative assets still need rights and quality review.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Do women with different bodies and backgrounds make consequential choices inside the simulated world?
Can women in the intended audience change the scenario's assumptions, rather than only react to a finished story?

title: Space Weather Modelling
oneLine: Make space-weather observations easier to compare, explain and connect to operational decisions.
need: People who depend on radio, navigation, satellites or power systems need understandable information about changing space conditions. The enterprise opportunity is not to promise that every disturbance can be predicted. It is to help a particular user interpret observations, uncertainty and the actions already defined by their responsible operators.
offer: Build an evidence-led dashboard or briefing workflow for one use case, with observation times, data provenance and uncertainty visible. Compare a simple historical baseline with any experimental model. Women entering science and data leadership could practise choosing metrics, explaining limitations and deciding whether a new model adds useful information.

firstPilot.title: Replay a historical event
steps: Choose a well-documented historical interval and one user decision the tool is intended to support.
Assemble public observations with their source, units, timestamps and missing-data notes.
Compare the existing reference approach with a simple experimental model using the same evaluation window.
Ask a domain expert and intended user whether the display changes understanding without overstating certainty.
firstPilot.deliverable: A reproducible event replay, model comparison and user-tested explanation of uncertainty.

evidence.known: Space-weather observations and forecasting services exist; this venture has not demonstrated an improved prediction method.
evidence.unknown: Whether the proposed approach adds useful lead time or decision value beyond established services.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Out-of-sample error, false alerts, missed events and the effect on the selected user decision.

businessModel: An educational analysis service or specialist workflow may be viable before a forecasting product. Any operational service needs independently assessed reliability.
leadershipDecision: Set the evidence threshold for a forecast claim and preserve negative results when a simpler model performs better.
risks: Historical fitting can exaggerate future performance.
Missing observations may look like calm conditions.
A research display can be mistaken for an operational warning service.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.

sources.title: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center products

equalityQuestions: Can women working in regional operations interpret uncertainty without a specialist beside them?
Who decides when a space-weather alert is worth interrupting a shift, and whose workload informs that choice?

title: Near Earth Object Mapping
oneLine: Help observers turn asteroid measurements into clear, traceable understanding of objects near Earth.
need: A moving point in a telescope image becomes useful knowledge only when measurements, timing, uncertainty and follow-up connect. This venture could help learners or small observatories understand that process. It should contribute to established scientific practice, with any hazard assessment left to the appropriate specialist systems.
offer: Build a public-data explorer or observation-preparation service that shows how an object's estimated path changes as evidence improves. Keep original catalogue identifiers and measurement provenance visible. Women leading the project would manage scientific quality, user education and the relationship between an engaging visualisation and an honest statement of uncertainty.

firstPilot.title: Follow one object's evidence trail
steps: Choose a well-documented object from a recognised public catalogue and collect its observation and orbit references.
Create a visual timeline showing additional measurements and uncertainty rather than only a smooth orbital line.
Have an astronomy specialist check coordinate, unit and time handling.
Test whether learners understand the difference between an observation, a fitted orbit and an impact-risk assessment.
firstPilot.deliverable: A reproducible public-data story and a checked observation-planning prototype.

evidence.known: NASA describes an established process of discovery, follow-up measurements and orbit computation. This concept would build on that work.
evidence.unknown: Which gap an additional tool can fill for a particular observatory or learning audience.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Reproduction of reference values and user understanding of uncertainty and data age.

businessModel: Explore an educational product, commissioned visualisation or observatory workflow service, with the customer and scientific review costs identified early.
leadershipDecision: Decide which results the team is qualified to interpret and which require referral to established monitoring services.
risks: A visual close approach could be misread as an impact threat.
Incorrect time or coordinate conversion can corrupt results.
Outdated records can give false confidence.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Can regional women and learners use the object explorer with ordinary equipment and accessible explanations?
Are women given scientific interpretation and data-quality authority as well as public-communication work?

title: 100K Solar System Satellite Web
oneLine: Work backwards from a useful observation to the smallest satellite network that could provide it.
need: The archive's 100,000-satellite title expresses solar-system ambition. A practical design process starts with an observation that matters, the people who need it and the limits of existing data. Network size is an outcome of the mission requirements, not a target that should override usefulness, cost or responsible operation.
offer: Create a mission-design workbench comparing purchased data, ground instruments, a single spacecraft and a small network. Model coverage, communications, power, data volume and failure recovery before considering larger constellations. The enterprise could first sell analysis, simulation or an instrument component with an independently testable requirement.

firstPilot.title: One observation requirement
steps: Choose one phenomenon to observe and define resolution, timing and acceptable data gaps.
Compare publicly available information with the proposed new measurement to establish the actual gap.
Simulate a small set of mission architectures and document every assumed input.
Ask an independent mission engineer to review the weakest link and specify a ground-based component test.
firstPilot.deliverable: A mission trade study, reproducible simulation and one component-level test brief.

evidence.known: Virtual Solar Swarm is a related design study, with teaching models rather than launched hardware.
evidence.unknown: Whether a new spacecraft or network is needed, and what architecture could satisfy the chosen requirement.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Useful observation coverage and data quality per complete mission cost under failure scenarios.

businessModel: Start with mission analysis, educational software or a qualified component. A large constellation would need separate customers, finance and mission authorisation.
leadershipDecision: Set a mission value test that can justify reducing the network dramatically when a simpler architecture works.
risks: Communications may constrain the network more than sensors.
Launch and replacement assumptions may be optimistic.
Illustrations can make an unbuilt system appear operational.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Who can challenge mission priorities and decide which observations would serve women and communities most usefully?
Could women outside established space organisations own and lead a defined instrument, analysis or operations contribution?

title: Off World Mining and Refining
oneLine: Turn off-world resource ambitions into material-handling experiments with clear terrestrial value.
need: Off-world mining asks more than whether a resource might exist. A mission needs a useful product, an extraction process, power, machinery, maintenance and a destination for the output. Each dependency can change the case. The first enterprise should identify a narrow technical problem worth solving even if a distant mining economy develops slowly.
offer: Explore remote material sorting, abrasive-dust handling or small-scale process monitoring using safe terrestrial simulants. Compare the proposed method with an existing industrial technique and record where space conditions would change the result. This creates a bridge between a speculative resource vision and a testable robotics or materials service.

firstPilot.title: A bench-top material-handling test
steps: Choose a single operation such as sorting particles or transferring abrasive material and define the intended output.
Select a safe, documented simulant and an existing method as the comparison.
Measure throughput, contamination, energy demand and equipment wear in controlled trials.
List the environmental differences that prevent the terrestrial result from proving space readiness.
firstPilot.deliverable: An experimental report, sample-handling record and next-stage test specification.

evidence.known: The source names off-world mining and refining as an ambition. It supplies no resource rights, mission or validated extraction system.
evidence.unknown: Whether the chosen method remains useful under remote operation, constrained power and difficult maintenance.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Usable output per energy input, wear rate and successful recovery from a blocked or failed operation.

businessModel: Develop a terrestrial testing or automation service first where justified. Space-specific contracts would depend on a customer's verified mission need.
leadershipDecision: Choose an experiment whose result remains valuable even if the larger off-world market does not arrive on the hoped-for schedule.
risks: A simulant may omit the hardest real conditions.
Maintenance assumptions can dominate reliability.
Demand for the extracted product remains hypothetical.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Can women in remote operations shape the test around maintenance and recovery tasks they understand?
Who would share ownership and decision-making power if the tested mining subsystem became commercially useful?

title: Earthquake/Volcano Prediction
oneLine: Improve hazard understanding while clearly separating earthquake prediction from monitoring and preparedness.
need: Communities benefit from understandable hazard information, but confident claims about the exact timing of earthquakes can mislead people. The archive combines earthquake and volcano prediction in one title; the venture must separate these different scientific problems and begin with a question qualified geoscientists consider answerable.
offer: Build a historical-data teaching or research tool that explains observations, uncertainty and official information routes. For earthquakes, frame work around hazard interpretation, research evaluation or early-warning education rather than promising exact forecasts. A volcano-focused project would need its own monitoring question, relevant observatory expertise and evidence standard.

firstPilot.title: A claim tested against a historical record
steps: Choose a narrowly stated research claim and document what would count as success before inspecting test data.
Separate training and evaluation periods and compare the claim with a simple baseline.
Include false alarms, missed events and data gaps in the results.
Ask an independent geoscientist to review the explanation and remove language implying a public warning capability.
firstPilot.deliverable: A reproducible evaluation, an accessible uncertainty explainer and a list of unsupported claims rejected.

evidence.known: USGS states that reliable prediction of a major earthquake's time, location and magnitude has not been achieved.
evidence.unknown: Whether a proposed signal adds any out-of-sample information beyond established hazard or monitoring approaches.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Predefined performance on unseen records, including the cost of false reassurance and frequent false alarms.

businessModel: Educational materials or transparent research-analysis services are possible starting offers. An operational warning product would need much stronger evidence and authority.
leadershipDecision: Commit to publishing a null result when the proposed method fails, even if the original story is attractive.
risks: Coincidence can be mistaken for prediction.
A research display could delay attention to official advice.
Combining different hazards can conceal invalid assumptions.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: What information do women coordinating homes, care or local services need when geological conditions are uncertain?
Can those affected define the costs of false reassurance and repeated alerts, rather than leaving success to a model score?

title: Quantum Computing Frameworks
oneLine: Help teams understand where quantum computing might fit, using honest comparisons with conventional methods.
need: A business can spend heavily on an exciting computational approach before defining the problem well enough to compare alternatives. This concept begins with a workload, its constraints and the best practical conventional method available to the team. Learning value and demonstrated performance should be reported separately.
offer: Develop a small benchmark and teaching framework that represents the same problem in classical and quantum-inspired or quantum forms. Record data preparation, solver assumptions, run conditions and total effort. The product would help a customer decide what to investigate, rather than claiming that a quantum label itself delivers a speed advantage.

firstPilot.title: One problem, transparent benchmarks
steps: Choose a small, relevant optimisation or simulation problem with a known way to check the answer.
Implement a clear conventional baseline and document its tuning and resource use.
Use a simulator or authorised computing service for the alternative approach, recording its limitations.
Have an independent reviewer reproduce the comparison and identify which conclusions do not generalise.
firstPilot.deliverable: A reproducible benchmark notebook, teaching notes and a decision brief for further research.

evidence.known: The catalogue proposes frameworks rather than a specified quantum machine, algorithm or proven advantage.
evidence.unknown: Whether a chosen approach offers a useful advantage on a meaningful workload after all overheads are counted.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Solution quality, full execution cost, reproducibility and scaling behaviour under comparable conditions.

businessModel: Training, benchmark design or technical evaluation could support an early service. Research claims should not be priced as guaranteed production savings.
leadershipDecision: Define what evidence would justify a larger research spend and when a conventional solution should be preferred.

Unequal benchmark effort can favour the desired answer.
Hardware access and repeated runs can alter cost.

title: Global Governance Networks
oneLine: Connect local decisions through transparent agreements, shared learning and accountable representation.
need: Groups working across places need ways to share knowledge without erasing local priorities. Large governance diagrams can hide basic unanswered questions: who may decide, whose consent is needed, how disagreements are handled and what happens when a group leaves. The opportunity is a usable coordination practice, starting with willing participants.
offer: Create a decision-record and meeting-support service for a small network of community or enterprise groups. Each group keeps its own authority while agreeing how shared work is proposed, reviewed and reported. AI may help summarise approved records, but participants must be able to correct them and see who is responsible for decisions.

firstPilot.title: Two groups, one shared decision
steps: Invite two willing groups to choose a practical shared task with a limited scope.
Write a plain-language agreement covering decision rights, information sharing, conflicts and withdrawal.
Run a facilitated decision process and record reasons, dissent and the person responsible for each action.
Review the experience with participants who spoke least and revise the process before adding more groups.
firstPilot.deliverable: An agreed decision template, a completed example and a revised coordination charter.

evidence.known: The current plan proposes growth through local choice, shared capability and actual working relationships. It does not establish a global governing authority.
evidence.unknown: Whether the process is understandable and legitimate to the people expected to use it.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Participant understanding of authority, actions completed and unresolved objections after the decision.

businessModel: A facilitation and governance-support service could be funded by participating organisations, with clear limits on the service provider's power.
leadershipDecision: Choose how to protect minority voices while still allowing useful decisions and timely delivery.
risks: Participation can become symbolic if authority is unclear.
Translation and access gaps may exclude people.
An AI summary can flatten disagreement.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.

What authority would local women retain if they disagree with a decision made elsewhere in the network?

title: Fukushima Extreme Robotics
oneLine: Build remote-handling capability for difficult environments without claiming access to Fukushima operations.
need: The Fukushima title points to demanding inspection and recovery work where equipment may face poor visibility, constrained access and dangerous conditions. The venture's starting point should be a safely reproduced handling problem. It must not imply a relationship with the facility, its operators or any nuclear clean-up programme.
offer: Develop a remotely operated inspection or retrieval capability in a non-hazardous mock environment. Focus on one useful feature such as recovering a stuck tool, operating with delayed feedback or navigating a cluttered space. The same carefully measured capability may have applications in industrial inspection and other inaccessible workplaces.

firstPilot.title: A difficult retrieval in a safe mock-up
steps: Define a non-hazardous mock task with dimensions, visibility limits and a clear success criterion.
Build or adapt a remote tool with a qualified robotics team and an independent emergency stop.
Run repeated trials, deliberately including loss of view, snagging and communication interruption.
Measure recovery success and document every condition not represented by the mock-up.
firstPilot.deliverable: A repeatable test rig, trial record and engineering brief for the next capability improvement.

evidence.known: The archive names extreme robotics in connection with Fukushima. It establishes no project access or validated radiation-tolerant machine.
evidence.unknown: Whether the tool can complete and recover from the chosen task reliably enough to justify specialised development.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Task completion, recovery rate, operator workload and equipment damage across repeated trials.

businessModel: Sell an inspection tool or testing service where a real customer has the specified need. Nuclear deployment requires its own authorised technical programme.
leadershipDecision: Set a clear boundary between what the safe mock-up demonstrates and what remains untested in extreme conditions.
risks: A mock-up may omit the dominant failure condition.
Recovery may be harder than the original task.
The historical name may imply an unauthorised affiliation.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Would women operators with varied hand sizes and reach be able to control and recover the robot comfortably?
Can operators reject a design that looks impressive but is difficult to use, and hold technical authority over its revision?

title: Subterranean City Building
oneLine: Break the underground-city vision into inspectable systems, human needs and decisions that can be tested.
need: An underground settlement would depend on geology, structure, air, water, power, access and a life people actually want. These systems cannot be made credible by drawing a large city all at once. A useful enterprise begins with a specific component or planning question and treats human experience as seriously as engineering.
offer: Develop a digital systems model and a full-size surface mock-up of one underground-like space. Examine a workshop, service corridor or shared room before making claims about habitation. Link the model to maintenance access, evacuation, everyday comfort and the consequences of losing a supporting service.

firstPilot.title: One space and its supporting services
steps: Choose a limited space and state who would use it, for how long and for what purpose.
Map every dependency, including ventilation, water, power, waste, communications and exit routes.
Build a surface mock-up or digital walk-through for access and maintenance review.
Run a service-failure exercise and publish the conditions that would make the concept unacceptable.
firstPilot.deliverable: A dependency model, reviewed spatial brief and next-test programme for one component.

evidence.known: The source includes autonomously built resilient cities as a long-term ambition. No inhabited underground city design is validated here.
evidence.unknown: Whether the proposed setting can provide an acceptable life and maintainable services at a defensible cost.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Unresolved dependencies, maintenance task access and performance of the chosen component test.

businessModel: Component design, simulation or maintenance planning may create practical enterprises before any city-scale project is justified.
leadershipDecision: Decide which human needs are non-negotiable and give prospective residents authority over the definition of an acceptable environment.
risks: Interdependent systems can fail together.
Construction images can conceal missing life-support assumptions.
Long-term upkeep may be underfunded.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: What would women want to control about daylight, private space, care and leaving an underground environment?
Are women maintaining the services involved in deciding repair access and acceptable working conditions?

title: Live Aid 2025 Cities >50K People
oneLine: Reinterpret the archive's city-scale Live Aid ambition as a practical network of locally led creative events.
need: The historical 2025 label records an earlier ambition, not a current event announcement. Large cultural programmes need local organisers, accessible venues, artists, production support and a clear purpose. A city population threshold is not a substitute for willingness, capacity or the needs of the audience.
offer: Explore a shared event-production kit that lets independent organisers contribute a local programme to a wider creative conversation. Begin with one willing host and one modest event. The kit could include scheduling, artist agreements, accessibility information, streaming choices and a transparent account of where proceeds or support are intended to go.

firstPilot.title: One hosted performance and a reusable kit
steps: Agree the purpose, audience and responsibilities with a willing organiser and venue.
Build a programme with paid roles, access needs, rehearsal time and a realistic production budget.
Run a small event or closed production rehearsal with a clear consent and recording process.
Publish the organiser-approved lessons and identify what another location could reuse.
firstPilot.deliverable: An event brief, production checklist and reviewed replication kit grounded in one real host's experience.

evidence.known: The catalogue's Live Aid 2025 wording is historical. No new date, artist, venue or connection to the established Live Aid organisation is confirmed.
evidence.unknown: Whether organisers want a shared network and which services would save them time or improve participation.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Audience access, artist and crew experience, delivery against the agreed budget and useful material reused.

businessModel: A production-support service, commissioned programme or shared resource subscription could be tested. Any fundraising purpose requires an identified recipient and agreed terms.
leadershipDecision: Choose a name, purpose and operating model that respect existing brands and keep local organisers in control.
risks: A historical title may imply an unconfirmed event.
Shared branding can overwhelm local authorship.
Volunteer enthusiasm can conceal unpaid production work.

title: Live Aid 2025 Artistic World Vote
oneLine: Explore fair audience participation that celebrates art without turning popularity into the only measure of value.
need: A global artistic vote sounds simple until languages, audience size, access, campaigning and different art forms are considered. The historical Live Aid 2025 title should remain identifiable as an archive concept. A current experiment can ask a smaller question: how can audiences meaningfully respond to creative work?
offer: Design a participation tool for a willing local showcase, comparing voting with discussion, peer appreciation and audience reflection. Artists should understand how their work is presented and how responses will be used. The product may become an accessible feedback service rather than a winner-takes-all global competition.
users: Audiences with varied access and language needs

firstPilot.title: A fair response process for one showcase
steps: Co-design the purpose and response options with participating artists before selecting a voting mechanism.
Test the interface with fictional entries, including low bandwidth and assistive technology.
Run a small showcase with transparent rules, clear consent and a way to report manipulation or mistakes.
Compare participation patterns and artist feedback to see whose work or audience the format disadvantaged.
firstPilot.deliverable: A tested audience-response prototype, fairness review and revised event rules.

evidence.known: The original title is an unimplemented historical proposal. No world vote, artist participation or official event affiliation is established.
evidence.unknown: Whether voting improves the experience or whether a different form of response better serves artists and audiences.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Participation diversity, comprehension of the rules, suspicious response patterns and artist-rated usefulness.

businessModel: Offer the tool and moderation service to event hosts. The price should cover accessibility, support and fair handling of disputes.
leadershipDecision: Decide what success means before counting votes, including whether competitive ranking belongs in the programme at all.
risks: Large followings can dominate merit or discovery.
Bots or coordinated voting can distort results.
Rankings may discourage experimental or minority-language work.

Can artists choose how their work is presented and challenge unfair voting or moderation decisions?

title: Tidal and Wave Power
oneLine: Find a coastal energy use that might justify careful testing of tidal or wave technology.
need: A coastal community may have energy needs that differ from those of a large grid customer. Marine equipment must also coexist with fishing, recreation, ecology and maintenance access. The founder's task is to compare an actual load with several supply options before selecting an attractive technology.
offer: Develop a site-neutral energy options study followed, if justified, by a small authorised test. Distinguish tidal flow from wave motion, and define which one the proposed device uses. Women in regional technical roles could lead load measurement, stakeholder discussions and service planning, with marine workers' experience shaping the design.

firstPilot.title: A load and resource comparison
steps: Select an energy use such as a shore facility and measure its demand over a representative period.
Use documented marine-resource information to estimate a range of possible output without claiming a site is available.
Compare marine options with efficiency, solar, storage and existing supply on a consistent basis.
Ask marine and electrical specialists to define the smallest authorised test that would resolve the main uncertainty.
firstPilot.deliverable: A comparative energy brief with a measurement plan and clear reasons to proceed or stop.

evidence.known: The planning catalogue proposes tidal and wave power; the related Straddie workbench is an options exploration, not an approved installation.
evidence.unknown: Whether the local resource and service requirements justify marine equipment over simpler alternatives.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Useful energy delivered against measured demand, including maintenance downtime and seasonal variation.

businessModel: An energy assessment or maintenance service may be the first viable offer. Device deployment depends on a separate engineering and operating case.
leadershipDecision: Choose performance criteria that include affordability, local work and marine use, not just peak device output.
risks: Access for repair may be weather-limited.
A short resource record may mislead.
Marine activities and ecological values may conflict with a proposed site.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.

Who would share the energy benefits, skilled work and decision-making power if an installation were eventually proposed?

title: Solar Desalination Bubbles
oneLine: Test whether a solar desalination concept can produce useful water with a manageable maintenance burden.
need: Remote and coastal users need water systems matched to source-water quality, daily demand and available skills. The archive's bubbles label is a concept name, not a defined device specification. A practical team would first decide what physical process is proposed and what water quality the intended use requires.
offer: Explore a small, instrumented desalination demonstrator with a qualified water specialist. Compare the proposed solar design with existing water supply and treatment options. The first product could be a monitoring, cleaning or maintenance service that improves an established system, especially where long trips for repairs make reliability more valuable than novelty.

firstPilot.title: A measured water-production trial
steps: Define the source water, intended use and target output with a qualified water professional.
Draw the proposed process, including heat input, fresh-water collection, concentrated residue and cleaning.
Run a controlled bench trial using appropriate equipment and independent water testing.
Compare useful output and labour with an established alternative under the same input conditions.
firstPilot.deliverable: A process diagram, measured trial results and a serviceability assessment.

evidence.known: The supplied title suggests solar desalination but does not establish a working bubble design or drinking-water performance.
evidence.unknown: Whether the chosen design provides worthwhile output after cleaning, residue handling and variable sunshine are included.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Verified water quality, usable water per energy input and maintenance time over repeated cycles.

businessModel: A small water-service or equipment-support business could be explored around a real customer. Potable supply requires its own verified treatment and operating arrangements.
leadershipDecision: Prioritise the user's ability to maintain and afford the system, including people far from specialist support.
risks: Clear-looking water may still fail the intended quality standard.
Residue handling can become the hidden problem.
Short trials may miss fouling and seasonal performance.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.

Who would do the cleaning and residue handling, and could those women influence the design and receive paid technical roles?

title: Mid Level Plasma Fusion
oneLine: Convert a fusion-energy ambition into a precise research question and an independently reviewable experiment.
need: Mid Level Plasma Fusion is an archive label without a complete technical definition. A credible venture would specify the physical mechanism, intended measurement and relationship to established fusion research. The goal of the first stage is knowledge, not an electricity sales promise or a locally improvised reactor.
offer: Develop an evidence map and research brief with a qualified plasma-physics group. Identify a modelling, sensing, materials or control problem that can be examined within an appropriately equipped institution. A service or component useful to researchers could be a more realistic first enterprise than a complete power-generation system.

firstPilot.title: An institution-led research definition
steps: Translate the archive title into a precise mechanism, operating assumptions and measurable question.
Review relevant primary research with a qualified specialist and distinguish demonstrated results from proposed improvements.
Select a simulation or institution-run component experiment with a documented comparison method.
Record the result, uncertainty and the next question without converting it into a claim of commercial power.
firstPilot.deliverable: A reviewed research brief, evidence table and costed request for the next institutional test.

evidence.known: The US Department of Energy describes remaining scientific and engineering challenges before fusion can reliably supply practical energy.
evidence.unknown: What the archive's mid-level approach specifically means and whether it identifies an advantage over existing research methods.
evidence.nextMeasurement: The selected physical or component metric, with full experimental conditions and uncertainty reported.

businessModel: Scientific software, diagnostics or specialist engineering may offer early customers. A power business would require evidence far beyond a conceptual study.
leadershipDecision: Decide whether the proposed mechanism warrants research funding after independent criticism, and preserve a clear stop condition.
risks: Ambiguous terminology can conceal an undefined mechanism.
A component result does not prove net electrical generation.
Specialist infrastructure and oversight may be substantial.

title: Pumped Water Storage
oneLine: Assess pumped water storage as one option for matching energy supply with the times people need it.
need: An energy system can have plenty of generation at the wrong time. Storage choices must fit the duration, power demand, land, water and operating conditions of a real user. The venture should ask which service is needed before assuming that reservoirs or a particular landscape should be developed.
offer: Build a transparent storage comparison using measured loads and explicitly hypothetical site parameters. Include the energy required for pumping, useful electricity returned, water management and the ability to maintain equipment. A local enterprise could provide analysis or operating support without taking on an unapproved civil works project.

firstPilot.title: Storage options for one measured load
steps: Gather an authorised demand record and define the hours of supply the customer needs.
Model pumped storage alongside demand shifting, batteries and existing supply using consistent assumptions.
Ask civil, electrical and water specialists to identify the constraints a real site would introduce.
Test sensitivity to water availability, efficiency, outages and maintenance costs before recommending further investigation.
firstPilot.deliverable: A storage comparison workbook and a site-assessment brief if the option remains promising.

evidence.known: The catalogue lists pumped water storage as a clean-power enterprise theme, with no site or engineering design supplied.
evidence.unknown: Whether the required service and local conditions make this option competitive or appropriate.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Delivered storage service, total energy losses and whole-life operating requirements across realistic scenarios.

businessModel: Offer independent storage assessment and operational planning. Construction revenue is a separate proposition requiring a defined customer, design and permissions.
leadershipDecision: Choose how water, landscape and community priorities are weighed alongside the energy calculation.
risks: A convenient elevation model may hide unsuitable ground conditions.
Water availability may change.
Civil costs can dominate a small installation.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.

Can women affected by the water, land and maintenance requirements influence the comparison before a preferred site is promoted?

title: Battery Technology
oneLine: Build a battery service around the job the customer needs done and the full life of the equipment.
need: Battery discussions often focus on a single specification while the customer needs dependable service, straightforward support and an affordable replacement path. A remote household, workshop and fleet depot may need different solutions. Body-friendly handling, clear controls and local technical jobs also belong in the design conversation.
offer: Explore a battery assessment, monitoring or maintenance-planning business before proposing a new cell chemistry. Compare existing products for a defined use, using manufacturer documentation and qualified electrical input. For a research route, define a specific material or performance question with a laboratory partner rather than presenting an untested chemistry as ready to sell.

firstPilot.title: A service-life comparison for one use
steps: Define the customer's load, outage tolerance, operating environment and available maintenance skills.
Compare suitable documented products using the same duty cycle and replacement assumptions.
Trial a monitoring or user-information prototype without altering electrical protection or live equipment.
Review support calls, data clarity and the plan for repair, replacement and end-of-life handling.
firstPilot.deliverable: A product-neutral service brief, monitoring prototype and life-cycle cost comparison.

evidence.known: Battery technology is a broad source theme; no new chemistry or validated product is claimed by this page.
evidence.unknown: Whether the strongest opportunity is product development, better installation support, monitoring or recovery of used equipment.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Useful service delivered, support burden, replacement assumptions and customer understanding of the system.

businessModel: Assessment, supported monitoring or maintenance coordination could generate service revenue. Include replacement planning and responsible end-of-life arrangements in the offer.
leadershipDecision: Choose a business model that rewards reliable service rather than unnecessary equipment sales.
risks: Product comparisons can omit incompatible operating conditions.
Poor support can leave remote users stranded.
Used equipment may have uncertain history or handling needs.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 15; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.

Would regional women have access to skilled maintenance roles and dependable help when equipment fails?

title: Superchargers
oneLine: Plan fast-charging access around real journeys, usable spaces and the local electricity supply.
need: Charging is part of a person's trip, not just a power rating. Drivers may need lighting, toilets, room for mobility aids, space to manoeuvre a large body or vehicle, and a place to wait with children. Regional and remote routes also require confidence about availability and help when a charger is unavailable.
offer: Develop a charging-service study for one location or fleet, combining demand, access design, queueing and electrical capacity. The venture could offer site planning, user information or maintenance coordination. Hardware selection should follow a clear description of the journey and the qualified assessment of the local supply.

firstPilot.title: A charging stop designed with users
steps: Map a real journey or fleet duty cycle and identify when charging would be useful.
Interview varied drivers about reaching controls, cable handling, waiting, toilets and personal comfort.
Model demand and queues against verified equipment and supply information with qualified electrical advice.
Test signs, status information and a non-electrical full-size layout before any installation decision.
firstPilot.deliverable: A user-tested site brief, demand model and service-response plan.

evidence.known: The archive uses the broad title Superchargers. It does not identify a supplier, brand partnership or approved charging site.
evidence.unknown: Whether enough users need the location and whether reliable operation can be provided at an acceptable cost.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Journey usefulness, accessible task completion, expected queues and response to equipment faults.

businessModel: Explore a host service agreement, charging operations support or fleet planning contract using verified tariffs and demand.
leadershipDecision: Choose access and reliability standards that serve the full audience, including people travelling after dark or far from alternatives.
risks: Grid connection costs may change the case.
An accessible bay can still have unusable controls or cables.
A failed charger can disrupt a long journey.
equalityQuestions: What makes a charging stop comfortable and usable for women travelling alone, with children or with mobility needs?
Who controls the site design and whose journey has been overlooked?

title: Solar Concentration Furnaces
oneLine: Match concentrated solar heat to a specific process before designing a furnace around it.
need: Some production processes need heat at particular temperatures and for particular periods. A solar furnace concept must be judged against that process, the local resource, controllability and backup requirements. The opportunity might lie in process design or testing rather than building a large new energy facility.
offer: Explore a qualified laboratory study of one thermal task such as materials testing or controlled drying. Define the required temperature profile, uniformity and product quality, then compare solar concentration with established heat sources. Women leading the enterprise could connect scientific measurement with practical workshop and customer requirements.

firstPilot.title: One heat requirement, measured properly
steps: Choose a process with a clear temperature-time requirement and a way to test the resulting product.
Map the energy input, optical control, heat losses and safe operating boundaries with specialists.
Use an appropriate research facility or a simulation before considering any physical concentrator trial.
Compare repeatability, useful output and operator effort with a conventional process.
firstPilot.deliverable: A thermal process brief, comparison results and a next-stage engineering question.

evidence.known: The source proposes solar concentration furnaces but supplies no validated furnace, temperature claim or process economics.

businessModel: A testing or process-integration service could be explored before selling equipment. Customers would need evidence tied to their actual production requirements.
leadershipDecision: Decide whether process reliability and operator usability justify the design, even if peak-temperature demonstrations are impressive.

Concentrated radiation requires specialist controls.
Backup and thermal storage may alter the economics.

title: Bladeless Wind Turbines
oneLine: Evaluate a bladeless wind concept against measured output and the needs of a real location.
need: A device with a different shape may solve a useful problem, but appearance alone says little about energy service. A proposed wind system needs a defined operating mechanism, resource conditions, maintenance plan and comparison with available alternatives. Community preferences about noise, appearance and access should be heard early.
offer: Create an independent evaluation framework for a specific bladeless design, starting with documentation and a qualified test plan. The enterprise could help customers compare emerging devices without becoming a promoter of unsupported performance claims. A practical first service might be local wind measurement and energy-use assessment.

firstPilot.title: A documented device comparison
steps: Ask the design owner to specify the operating mechanism, rated conditions and test evidence.
Define a customer load and compare the device with other supply options under the same resource assumptions.
Have an independent specialist design a suitable controlled test or review existing measured data.
Report net useful output, downtime and uncertainty, including cases where the device is not appropriate.

A distinctive design may still be difficult to maintain.

Can women users and maintainers challenge output claims and compare the device with simpler alternatives?

title: Gravity Power
oneLine: Treat gravity as a possible energy-storage mechanism, with every input and loss counted.
need: The title Gravity Power can be misunderstood as energy without an input. This proposal should instead define a storage or mechanical process in which energy enters, is held and is later recovered. A good first study makes the accounting visible and asks whether the service is useful compared with alternatives.
offer: Build a transparent model of a specified lifting, lowering or water-based storage system for a defined load. Compare it with other storage methods using the same duration, power and maintenance assumptions. If a physical demonstration is worthwhile, it should be a controlled educational model designed by competent people, not a claim of free energy.

firstPilot.title: An energy-accounting demonstrator
steps: Write a complete input-to-output diagram for the proposed mechanism and identify every energy source.
Model a small storage duty using documented component assumptions and explicit losses.
Compare the result with pumped water storage, batteries or demand shifting for the same service.
Have an independent engineer review the accounting and specify any safe demonstrator that would add evidence.
firstPilot.deliverable: A checked energy balance, comparison model and a clear explanation of the proposed storage service.

evidence.known: The archive supplies a broad title, not a self-powered machine or a proven new storage system.
evidence.unknown: Whether the proposed geometry and machinery can deliver a useful storage service at competitive whole-life cost.

leadershipDecision: Reject any business claim that leaves its energy input or operating losses unexplained.

Moving masses require careful mechanical design.
Civil works and maintenance may overwhelm small-scale benefits.

Could women maintaining the system shape lifting machinery, controls and recovery arrangements from the start?

title: Hydrogen
oneLine: Explore hydrogen only where a specific customer's need survives comparison with direct electricity and other options.

The strongest starting point is a defined customer requirement, not a colour label or a large production target. Regional communities also need to understand who receives the benefits, who operates the system and what skills remain locally.
offer: Develop a customer-led comparison of hydrogen and alternative ways to provide one industrial or transport service. Map the full chain and ask where losses, costs and handling requirements accumulate. An early venture may provide analysis, monitoring or specialist maintenance through qualified partners rather than producing fuel.

firstPilot.title: One end use and a complete supply chain
steps: Specify the customer's actual service requirement, operating hours and acceptable interruptions.
Draw each production, conditioning, storage, transport and use step for the proposed hydrogen route.
Compare the route with direct electrification and other credible options using consistent boundaries.
Obtain specialist review of the assumptions, handling needs and the largest unanswered cost or performance question.
firstPilot.deliverable: A whole-chain options brief and a targeted request for further measurement or supplier evidence.

evidence.known: Hydrogen is an original enterprise theme. The supplied material establishes no plant, offtake agreement or validated production cost.

leadershipDecision: Choose a customer problem that genuinely requires this route and explain why simpler alternatives are insufficient.
risks: A cheap production estimate may omit delivery costs.
Customer demand may not become a binding commitment.
Specialist operation and emergency arrangements may be extensive.
