Can women doing production help decide the operating routine and share ownership of any resulting enterprise?

title: Seafood
oneLine: Build a seafood service that connects reliable supply, care for waterways and a product customers value.
need: Seafood ideas can involve farming, harvesting, processing or distribution, each with distinct skills and constraints. A community may need better cold-chain coordination or market access before it needs a new production site. Local knowledge and women's existing work in food, business and marine livelihoods should shape the starting question.
offer: Explore one seafood product and its journey from an authorised supplier to a willing customer. Identify losses, handling requirements, traceability and service gaps. A practical venture might improve ordering, processing coordination or delivery while a more ambitious aquaculture proposal receives separate ecological and engineering review.

firstPilot.title: Trace one product to its customer
steps: Agree a product and quality specification with an authorised supplier and prospective buyer.
Map the cold chain, packaging, handling and handovers using the supplier's established food-safety system.
Test a small ordering or logistics improvement under the responsible operator's control.
Measure accepted deliveries, unsold product, handling time and whether the buyer would repeat the order.
firstPilot.deliverable: A traceable supply-chain brief and a tested service improvement.

evidence.known: Seafood is a source enterprise theme; no aquaculture lease, harvest authority or operating partnership is implied.
evidence.unknown: Whether the main opportunity is new production or better coordination of an existing lawful supply chain.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Product acceptance, delivery reliability, avoidable loss and margin after all handling costs.

resources: Food-safety and marine expertise as relevant
businessModel: A logistics, ordering or processing-support service may be tested with existing operators. New aquaculture requires a distinct site and production case.
leadershipDecision: Choose an offer that respects local livelihoods and establishes who carries the risk when product is delayed or rejected.
risks: Cold-chain failures can undermine the whole service.
Demand may fluctuate seasonally.
A production proposal can conflict with ecological or existing-use priorities.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Which seafood ordering and delivery changes would save women time without shifting unpaid work onto someone else?
Are women in the existing supply chain included in price, quality and ownership decisions?

title: Seaweed
oneLine: Find a useful seaweed product by starting with the buyer, the species and the whole growing system.
need: Seaweed is often presented as one solution to many problems, but food, extracts, feed and materials have different evidence and quality requirements. A credible business chooses one use and asks how a suitable product can be grown or sourced, processed and delivered without assuming access to coastal waters.
offer: Develop a product-and-supply study with an authorised grower or qualified research partner. Compare an existing material or ingredient with a documented seaweed sample. The first enterprise may be processing, quality testing or market development, while any new cultivation system follows a separate environmental and operating assessment.

firstPilot.title: One seaweed sample, one product question
steps: Select one intended use and obtain the buyer's required characteristics and evidence needs.
Source a traceable sample through an appropriate existing producer or research partner.
Test the relevant product property with qualified analysis rather than making broad environmental or health claims.
Map processing losses, storage, transport and the likely route to a repeat customer.
firstPilot.deliverable: A sample-based product brief, supply map and next-test decision.

evidence.known: The catalogue proposes seaweed within closed-loop food. It does not identify a species, farm, verified benefit or available growing area.
evidence.unknown: Whether a particular seaweed product meets a buyer's needs consistently and at a viable delivered cost.
evidence.nextMeasurement: The selected product property, batch consistency, accepted yield and buyer response.

businessModel: Test ingredient supply, processing or product-development services before funding a new farm. Avoid depending on several unverified revenue streams at once.
leadershipDecision: Choose the primary product claim and require evidence for it before adding environmental or health benefits to the pitch.
risks: Properties vary with species and growing conditions.
Drying and transport can dominate costs.
An attractive cultivation map does not establish permission or ecological suitability.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: What does the intended woman customer want from this seaweed ingredient or material?
Can women growers and processors influence quality requirements, seasonal workload and how added value is shared?

title: Superfoods
oneLine: Turn the broad superfoods label into a clearly described, enjoyable and honestly marketed food product.
need: People want food that fits their tastes, time, culture, income and nutritional needs. A fashionable label can distract from those practical requirements. The business should begin with a specific eating occasion and an actual product, with any nutrition claim reviewed against appropriate evidence and current requirements.
offer: Explore a convenient food product with a qualified food team and a varied group of customers. Include women working shifts, caring for families, living remotely or combining several jobs. The product might succeed because it is affordable, tasty and easy to store rather than because it promises exceptional health effects.

firstPilot.title: A real eating occasion
steps: Ask customers to describe one difficult meal or snack occasion, including taste, cost, access and preparation time.
Co-design a small number of product options using a qualified food-development partner.
Run an authorised tasting with clear ingredient and allergen information and accessible feedback.
Compare repeat interest, preparation effort, packaging and full production costs.
firstPilot.deliverable: A tested product brief, honest description and a next-batch decision.

evidence.known: Superfoods is an archive category title, not evidence that a particular ingredient prevents or treats a condition.
evidence.unknown: Which product customers would regularly buy and whether its convenience and price remain attractive beyond a first tasting.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Repeat purchase intent tested against an actual price, sensory feedback and production consistency.

businessModel: Explore a small product line, contract manufacturing or a food-service offer. Base the case on repeat use and viable production, not exaggerated health claims.
leadershipDecision: Decide what promise the product can honestly make and how affordability will be protected as it develops.
risks: Health language can outrun the evidence.
Premium ingredients may exclude the intended audience.
A product loved in a tasting may not fit everyday routines.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Would the food suit women managing shifts, care, remote shopping or limited storage at a price they would choose?
Can the marketing describe a useful product without judging women's bodies or promising exceptional health outcomes?

title: Mushrooms and Fungi
oneLine: Explore fungi through one controlled product pathway, from growing conditions to a customer who needs the result.
need: Mushrooms and fungi suggest food, materials and research opportunities, but each requires a different production and quality system. A founder must choose the intended output and a qualified partner before turning spare organic material into a growing trial. Reliable batches and safe handling matter more than a striking demonstration.
offer: Develop a food-product or material-sample study using an established producer or laboratory. Compare the selected output with its current alternative and record substrate requirements, labour, contamination losses and storage. The venture might provide production services, materials testing or local distribution rather than immediately opening a grow facility.

firstPilot.title: A documented batch and customer test
steps: Choose either an edible product or a material application and write its acceptance criteria.
Work with an appropriate established grower or laboratory using documented inputs and procedures.
Track one batch from input to accepted output, including rejected material and labour.
Ask a buyer to evaluate the sample and identify what would be required for a repeat order.
firstPilot.deliverable: A batch record, customer evaluation and practical production brief.

evidence.known: The source lists mushrooms and fungi as a closed-loop theme. It does not establish a safe substrate, edible species or certified material.
evidence.unknown: Whether a consistent output can be produced at a useful scale with manageable contamination and labour.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Accepted yield, batch variation, production time and buyer-defined product performance.

businessModel: A supply partnership, production-support service or tested material product could be explored. Separate food and material pathways clearly in the business case.
leadershipDecision: Choose one application and quality system rather than making every potential fungal use part of the first enterprise.
risks: Contamination can disrupt production.
A waste stream may be an unsuitable input.
Material strength or food quality may vary between batches.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Can women working with the chosen fungi output shape handling, cleaning and inspection around their real needs?
Who receives credit and ownership for practical growing or processing knowledge that improves the product?

title: Legumes
oneLine: Build convenient legume products and supply relationships around how people actually cook and eat.
need: A familiar crop can still support a useful enterprise when preparation, packaging, distribution or cultural fit is improved. The question is not whether legumes are fashionable, but whether a particular customer needs a product that saves time, tastes good and fits their budget. Growers and food makers need dependable demand as well.
offer: Explore a ready-to-use ingredient, shared meal component or local procurement service with existing growers and food businesses. Invite customers from different household sizes, cultural backgrounds and work patterns. Women with cooking, farming or community-organising experience can lead product decisions and retain credit for the knowledge they contribute.

firstPilot.title: From a cooking problem to a repeat order
steps: Choose a specific cooking task customers find inconvenient and document what they use now.
Develop a sample with qualified food support, including packaging, storage and clear ingredient information.
Test preparation time, taste and portion usefulness with a varied customer group.
Offer a small authorised repeat-order trial and compare actual uptake with initial enthusiasm.
firstPilot.deliverable: A product specification, customer-use results and a supplier-to-buyer operating plan.

evidence.known: Legumes are an original food-enterprise suggestion. No particular product, nutrition outcome or supply contract is established.
evidence.unknown: Whether a convenient product can command enough repeat demand to cover preparation, packaging and distribution.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Repeat orders, preparation time saved, accepted product quality and avoidable waste.

businessModel: Explore prepared ingredients, wholesale supply or a subscription through an existing licensed operator, using actual order sizes and delivery costs.
leadershipDecision: Decide how customer affordability and producer returns will be balanced, especially where transport makes regional food expensive.
risks: Packaging can erase apparent savings.
Small orders may make distribution uneconomic.
One recipe or portion size may not suit the intended community.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Would the legume product save preparation time while fitting women's own food traditions, tastes and budgets?
Are women contributing recipes, growing knowledge or community relationships paid and included in product decisions?

title: Bacteria and Viruses
oneLine: Give the broad microbes theme a precise, professionally supervised research or food-production purpose.
need: Bacteria and viruses are a vast scientific field, not a single product concept. The first task is to select an appropriate, beneficial application and identify the expertise and oversight it requires. A food-fermentation service, data-analysis tool and virology research programme would have very different scope and responsibilities.
offer: Begin with a low-risk, established food-fermentation or laboratory-data question through a qualified partner. A practical enterprise could improve batch records, quality monitoring or public understanding. Any work involving viruses or unfamiliar organisms belongs within an authorised professional research setting, with no assumption that community experimentation is suitable.

firstPilot.title: A traceable fermentation data workflow
steps: Choose an established process with a qualified operator and define one record-keeping or quality question.
Use existing authorised records or a routine supervised batch rather than introducing unfamiliar organisms.
Prototype a dashboard that preserves measurements, operator notes and deviations.
Ask the responsible professional to compare the tool with the current process and identify errors or missing context.
firstPilot.deliverable: A checked data workflow and a precisely scoped next research or service brief.

evidence.known: The archive names bacteria and viruses but does not specify an organism, laboratory, protocol or validated product.
evidence.unknown: Which application is intended and whether a new tool contributes useful value beyond established practice.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Record completeness, detection of known deviations and operator time without weakening quality oversight.

businessModel: A laboratory or production software service may be a feasible first offer. Biological product development would require its own evidence and authorised facilities.
leadershipDecision: Define the scientific scope and responsible institution before raising support for any organism-based work.
risks: A broad title can hide incompatible applications.
A software pattern may be mistaken for a biological conclusion.
Unreviewed health claims could mislead customers.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Can women technicians define which fermentation record or quality-monitoring problem needs solving?
Are scientific judgement, routine quality work and accessible training valued in the enterprise's paid roles and ownership?

title: Poultry
oneLine: Improve a poultry enterprise through animal care, useful production records and dependable local demand.
need: Poultry businesses connect daily animal care, feed, housing, labour, product handling and customers. A new venture should start with a clearly defined improvement in an existing authorised operation. Women already doing farm and household work may hold valuable practical knowledge without having equivalent ownership or decision rights.
offer: Explore a service that improves scheduling, records, product distribution or equipment usability for a willing operator. The aim could be fewer missed tasks, clearer costs or better access to a local market. Any change affecting animal health or production practice should be reviewed by the appropriate qualified advisers.

firstPilot.title: One daily workflow improved
steps: Observe a routine with a willing operator and record the people, equipment and information it requires.
Choose one practical bottleneck such as task handover, packing records or order coordination.
Prototype a simple tool and test it within the operator's existing animal-care and food-handling arrangements.
Review workload, product losses, customer reliability and who gained time or authority.
firstPilot.deliverable: A tested farm-service improvement and a costed support offer.

evidence.known: Poultry is a catalogue theme. No farm, production system, animal-health claim or market commitment is supplied.
evidence.unknown: Whether the selected workflow improvement is valuable enough for operators to pay for and continue using.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Missed tasks, labour time, product rejection and repeat customer orders.

businessModel: Farm administration, distribution support or equipment-service contracts may be explored before starting a new production operation.
leadershipDecision: Agree how the people doing daily care will influence the system and share in productivity or ownership gains.
risks: A poorly fitted tool can add work.
Production disruptions can affect animal welfare and supply.
Informal family labour may be left out of costs.
equalityQuestions: Who performs the daily care and who controls farm income and investment?
Would this system give women more time and authority, or simply more reporting work?
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.

title: Medicinal Plants and Spices
oneLine: Develop plant and spice products with traceable ingredients, respectful knowledge use and evidence matched to the claim.
need: Medicinal Plants and Spices combines everyday food with potential health-related uses. Those pathways must be separated. A culinary product can be developed around flavour and convenience, while a therapeutic claim requires appropriate evidence and professional review. Traditional or community knowledge cannot be treated as free raw material for a brand.
offer: Explore a traceable culinary ingredient, growing service or educational product with willing knowledge holders and qualified food support. Begin with a specific customer use and agreed sourcing. Where a medicinal research question is proposed, define it through a suitable professional institution without promising treatment or encouraging self-experimentation.

firstPilot.title: A culinary product with a clear provenance trail
steps: Choose a culinary use and document where the ingredient and associated knowledge come from.
Agree permissions, credit and benefit arrangements with any contributors whose knowledge is used.
Develop and test a sample through an appropriate food-production partner.
Review flavour, storage, traceability and the accuracy of every public product claim.
firstPilot.deliverable: A sample product, sourcing record and agreed description that makes only supportable claims.

evidence.known: The catalogue provides the theme, not evidence that a named plant treats a condition or that cultural knowledge may be commercialised.
evidence.unknown: Whether the product has repeat demand and a reliable, ethically agreed supply.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Customer use, batch consistency, traceability completeness and repeat purchase at an actual price.

businessModel: Culinary products, growing services or commissioned education may be explored. A medicinal product is a separate development and evidence pathway.
leadershipDecision: Decide which claims the venture can support and how contributors retain control, credit and a fair share of value.
risks: Culinary and therapeutic messages can become blurred.
Plant identity and quality may vary.
Knowledge may be used without meaningful agreement.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Who decides whether contributed plant knowledge may be used, credited, paid for or kept out of the product?
Would women customers receive clear information without pressure to accept unproven health or beauty claims?

title: Food Compute/Produce DAO
oneLine: Coordinate food demand and production through a practical shared planning service.
need: Growers, kitchens and customers may struggle with changing demand, small orders and information arriving too late. The archive uses the DAO label, but the useful starting question is who needs to coordinate what. A shared spreadsheet and clear human agreement may reveal the problem before any new platform is justified.
offer: Explore a cooperative planning tool that matches expected demand with available produce, processing and delivery capacity. Give producers and buyers clear control over their own information and commitments. The business should make uncertainty visible, distinguish an expression of interest from an order and keep responsibility for food quality with the proper operator.

firstPilot.title: A shared weekly demand plan
steps: Invite a few willing producers and buyers to define one product group and a common planning period.
Record supply estimates, demand, delivery constraints and who may see or change each entry.
Run a manual coordination cycle before automating it, documenting changes and unfilled orders.
Compare waste, coordination time and delivery reliability with participants' previous process.
firstPilot.deliverable: A tested planning template, participant agreement and evidence of where software could help.

evidence.known: The original title includes DAO. This proposed pilot is a human-governed coordination service and does not require a token or automated financial system.
evidence.unknown: Whether enough participants share compatible needs and will maintain accurate information.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Confirmed orders fulfilled, forecast error, avoidable surplus and coordinator hours.

businessModel: A membership or coordination fee could cover the service if it creates measurable value. Agree who owns the tool and how participants can leave with their records.
leadershipDecision: Choose a fair way to allocate scarce supply and share coordination costs without privileging the largest buyer.
risks: Forecasts may be mistaken for binding orders.
Small producers may carry disproportionate reporting work.
Commercially sensitive information may be exposed.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Can women producers choose their commitments and correct forecasts without being penalised by an opaque system?
Who is paid for maintaining shared food information and coordinating deliveries, and who controls the service?

title: Plastics and Glass
oneLine: Build a recovery business around clean material streams and customers who can use them.
need: Plastics and glass are broad material families with different collection, sorting and processing needs. A pile of discarded material is not yet a product. The venture must identify a consistent input, a customer specification and the work required to bridge the two, including transport that may be costly in regional communities.
offer: Explore one local stream such as a particular packaging type or a clean glass fraction with an authorised waste operator. Compare repair, reuse and material recovery before choosing machinery. Women could lead procurement, quality assurance and ownership design as well as collection and sorting, with physically usable equipment for varied bodies.
users: Local businesses producing a consistent stream

firstPilot.title: One material, one buyer
steps: Characterise a representative authorised sample by material type, contamination and available volume.
Ask a prospective buyer for its acceptance specification and minimum practical order.
Trial sorting or preparation through an appropriate existing operator, recording rejects and labour.
Compare revenue and avoided costs with transport, processing, quality testing and residual disposal.
firstPilot.deliverable: A material-flow brief, buyer-tested sample and a realistic recovery decision.

evidence.known: The source groups plastics and glass as a recovery theme. It supplies no verified processing method, customer or facility authority.
evidence.unknown: Whether a consistent saleable output can be produced locally at a better total outcome than current handling.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Accepted output, contamination, labour per unit and full delivered cost.

businessModel: Collection, preparation, reuse sales or a processing service may be viable for a particular stream. Avoid assuming all collected material has positive value.
leadershipDecision: Choose the stream and customer before equipment, and agree how workers benefit from safer, more productive handling.
risks: Mixed inputs can destroy product value.
Freight may outweigh local processing benefits.
Unsold output can become a new stockpile.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Would women sorting the material be able to use the bins, benches and lifting arrangements comfortably?
Can those doing collection and quality work influence the sale terms and share in the value recovered?

title: Nuclear Waste and Water
oneLine: Create a precise, institution-led research pathway for nuclear-waste and water questions.
need: The title Nuclear Waste and Water combines sensitive technical problems that require specialised authority, facilities and expertise. It is not a community treatment instruction or a claim that an untested method can make hazardous material harmless. The first useful work is to define one question and the evidence needed to examine it.
offer: Explore a research-support enterprise focused on data management, remote inspection, measurement interpretation or a non-hazardous materials test. Work through an authorised institution and keep each material category and treatment claim distinct. A founder could build a valuable tool for specialists without handling radioactive material or making unsupported remediation promises.

firstPilot.title: A non-hazardous research-support demonstrator
steps: Ask a qualified institution to define a narrow documentation, sensing or remote-handling problem.
Use public records, synthetic data or a non-hazardous simulant that the institution considers appropriate.
Build a traceable prototype and record what its test conditions do and do not represent.
Obtain independent review of the result before proposing any specialist deployment.
firstPilot.deliverable: A reviewed prototype, evidence record and clearly bounded institutional test request.

evidence.known: The archive supplies the theme only. It establishes no nuclear-waste treatment process, licence, access or proof of decontamination.
evidence.unknown: Which specific institutional need the venture can meet and what testing would establish useful performance.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Accuracy, traceability or remote-task performance against the institution's defined reference case.

resources: Controlled data or non-hazardous test materials
businessModel: Specialist software, documentation or instrument-support contracts may be a starting point. Hazardous-material operations are outside this pilot.
leadershipDecision: Choose a useful support function with explicit technical boundaries and refuse claims that exceed the test evidence.
risks: Different hazards can be wrongly treated as one problem.
A proxy test may not represent real operating conditions.
The subject can invite exaggerated treatment claims.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Can women with technical and field experience define the specialist nuclear documentation or inspection task?
Who can challenge a remediation claim, and are supporting technicians given authority as well as responsibility?

title: Industrial Process Byproducts
oneLine: Match one industrial byproduct to a real customer specification and an honest material balance.
need: Industrial leftovers vary in chemistry, consistency, contamination and handling cost. Calling them resources does not establish a safe or profitable use. A useful enterprise identifies one producer and one possible application, then tests the material and the customer's requirements before promising a closed loop.
offer: Develop a byproduct exchange or technical assessment service for a documented stream. Keep material identity, ownership, transport and acceptance conditions clear. The first value may come from better information or avoiding an unsuitable reuse, while a qualified materials partner determines whether processing can create a reliable input for another industry.

firstPilot.title: A documented stream-to-product match
steps: Obtain authorised material information and a representative sample from a willing producer.
Ask a potential user to define the property limits and evidence required for acceptance.
Commission suitable testing and compare the sample with the user's existing input.
Prepare the full handling, processing, transport and rejected-material account.
firstPilot.deliverable: A tested material specification and a buyer-producer decision brief.

evidence.known: The planning title normalises the archive's spelling to Industrial Process Byproducts. No particular stream or validated reuse is specified.
evidence.unknown: Whether the stream is consistent enough and whether the proposed use remains suitable after testing and delivered costs.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Specification compliance, batch variability, accepted yield and complete handling cost.

businessModel: Charge for characterisation, matching or processing services where value is demonstrated. Contracts should state who is responsible for rejected or changing material.
leadershipDecision: Decide when the evidence supports reuse and when a proposed loop should be rejected rather than marketed as circular.
risks: A small sample may not represent ongoing production.
Processing can transfer contamination into a new product.
Liability and ownership may be unclear at handover.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Are women managing the byproduct stream involved in deciding what extra sorting, storage or transport work is realistic?
How would the producer, receiving business and workers share any value created by the exchange?

title: Solid Waste Refuse Tips
oneLine: Turn one recoverable waste stream into a practical local service with clear authority and customers.
need: A refuse site contains many different materials and operational responsibilities. A community venture should not treat it as freely available stock. The useful starting point is an agreement with the responsible operator about one stream, a clear recovery task and a destination that genuinely wants the result.
offer: Explore a repair, reuse or recovery service alongside an authorised operator. The service could focus on a specific product type, visitor guidance or preparation for an established processor. Design jobs and tools for varied bodies and experience levels, and offer paid progression into technical, operations and leadership roles.

firstPilot.title: A small authorised recovery lane
steps: Agree access, responsibilities and a single material or product stream with the site operator.
Record volume, condition, handling needs and what currently happens to the stream.
Test sorting, repair or preparation in an appropriate workspace with qualified supervision.
Confirm actual customer acceptance and calculate labour, transport and residual disposal costs.
firstPilot.deliverable: An operator-approved workflow and a service case based on accepted recovered output.

evidence.known: The related Straddie Tip Loop Lab is a public proposal. It does not grant site access, council endorsement or waste-operation authority.
evidence.unknown: Which stream offers consistent value and whether recovery improves the full local outcome.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Items or material accepted for reuse, worker time, rejected fractions and net service cost.

businessModel: A recovery service contract, repair income or reuse sales may support the venture. Use observed supply and sales rather than theoretical waste value.
leadershipDecision: Choose a scope that the team can handle well and make worker safety, pay and advancement part of the operating model.
risks: Unclear authority can interrupt the service.
Recovered stock may not sell.
Handling and storage requirements may be underestimated.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: What would make the repair or recovery job accessible to women with varied strength, bodies and experience?
Can women progress from collection and sorting into paid technical, operational and ownership roles?

title: Human Waste and Life Support
oneLine: Design sanitation and resource-recovery services around health, dignity, maintainability and the people using them.
need: Human waste and life support connect toilets, water, treatment, maintenance and everyday dignity. Women may have different requirements across menstruation, pregnancy, caring, disability and ageing, while individuals' preferences differ. The venture should ask users what works and what fails before choosing a treatment technology.
offer: Explore an accessible sanitation-service brief for a specific facility or remote setting with qualified professionals. Begin with user journeys, maintenance responsibilities and reliable existing options. A resource-recovery idea can be considered only after the primary service and its treatment requirements are clearly defined and independently assessed.

firstPilot.title: A dignified facility and service plan
steps: Invite users to describe privacy, changing, washing, disposal, access and assistance needs in their own terms.
Map the full sanitation service with qualified advisers, including cleaning, breakdowns and collection or treatment.
Test a non-operating full-size layout with varied users and maintenance staff.
Compare suitable existing service options and identify what evidence any new treatment concept would need.
firstPilot.deliverable: A user-tested layout, maintenance plan and professional treatment-options brief.

evidence.known: The catalogue supplies a life-support theme, not a validated sanitation or resource-recovery system.
evidence.unknown: Which design best meets the selected users' needs while providing reliable, affordable maintenance.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Accessible task completion, privacy and comfort feedback, maintenance access and service continuity.

businessModel: Facility design, inspection coordination or maintenance support could form a service business. Treatment operations require a separately verified system and authorised provider.
leadershipDecision: Treat dignity and usability as essential service requirements, with the people using and cleaning the facility sharing design authority.
risks: A clever recovery idea can distract from basic sanitation.
Poor maintenance can undermine the whole system.
One standard cubicle may exclude many bodies and support needs.
equalityQuestions: What do women need for privacy, periods, pregnancy, feeding, changing and assisted care in this setting?
Who gets to set the design priorities and who will maintain the service?
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.

title: Farming Process Byproducts
oneLine: Find a useful second life for one farm byproduct without creating extra unpaid work or an unreliable market.
need: Farm residues differ by season, location, moisture, contamination and existing use. A proposed recovery business needs to understand what the material already does in the farming system before removing it. Farmers also need a service that fits busy periods and pays for the handling work it creates.
offer: Explore one stream with a willing farm and a defined buyer or processor. Compare keeping the material in its current use with transport, processing and an alternative product. Women doing farm administration, physical work and care should help determine the workflow, price and ownership arrangements, including whether the venture creates time or consumes it.
users: Buyers of a specified recovered product

firstPilot.title: A seasonal material-flow study
steps: Document the stream's volume, timing, condition and current role with the farm operator.
Obtain a prospective buyer's specification and identify necessary testing or preparation.
Trial a small authorised collection or sample-processing run through suitable partners.
Record all labour, transport, storage losses and consequences for the original farm operation.
firstPilot.deliverable: A seasonal supply brief and a tested decision on one recovery route.

evidence.known: The current planning title is Farming Process Byproducts. No feedstock, crop, buyer or recovery outcome is established.
evidence.unknown: Whether the stream can be collected consistently and whether its alternative use improves the farm's full situation.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Accepted output, seasonal availability, additional farm labour and net return after complete costs.

businessModel: A collection, processing or coordination fee can be explored where the service provides measurable value. Agree how farm labour and rejected loads are paid for.
leadershipDecision: Choose a recovery route that respects the farm's existing needs and does not make invisible household labour subsidise the business.
risks: Seasonal supply may not match buyer demand.
Removal may conflict with an existing beneficial use.
Long transport distances can erase returns.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Would the proposed use of farm byproducts free women's time or add another unpaid job during a busy season?
Can women doing practical and administrative farm work influence the price, schedule and ownership arrangement?

title: Subterranean City Displaced Muck
oneLine: Plan excavated-material handling before a major underground project creates the material.
need: Excavation produces material that must be characterised, moved, stored and either used or disposed of appropriately. The phrase displaced muck can hide major differences between clean rock, soil, mixed material and contaminated ground. An underground-city vision therefore needs a material plan before construction quantities become a persuasive headline.
offer: Develop a scenario-based material-flow tool for a hypothetical excavation or an authorised existing project. Link expected geology and uncertainty to testing, transport and possible receiving uses. A practical business could provide documentation, logistics analysis or materials matching, with qualified professionals determining suitability.

firstPilot.title: A transparent excavation-material scenario
steps: Select a documented or explicitly hypothetical excavation geometry and state the geological assumptions.
Estimate material quantities as ranges and identify where sampling would change the plan.
Compare potential receiving uses with their acceptance requirements and transport routes.
Run scenarios for unsuitable material, delayed receiving capacity and changes in excavation rate.
firstPilot.deliverable: A material-flow model, sampling brief and logistics risk register.

evidence.known: The catalogue links displaced material to a speculative subterranean-city programme. It establishes no excavation, material classification or receiving site.
evidence.unknown: What material would actually be encountered and whether a suitable, timely destination exists for it.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Quantity uncertainty, accepted reuse fraction, storage demand and logistics cost under changing conditions.

businessModel: Material-planning and logistics services can be explored with real civil projects independently of the larger city vision.
leadershipDecision: Require receiving capacity and material acceptance evidence before counting reuse as a project benefit.
risks: Ground conditions can change unexpectedly.
Stockpiles may grow when receiving sites are unavailable.
Assumed clean material may need different handling.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Can women living along proposed transport routes influence operating hours, access and assumptions in the material-flow model?
Are women doing sampling, documentation and logistics given paid time and a voice in decisions about destinations?

title: Mining Process Byproducts
oneLine: Evaluate mining byproducts with measured material properties and a customer-defined use.
need: A mining byproduct can contain useful material, unwanted constituents or both. The economic and environmental result depends on its specific properties, history and handling needs. A responsible venture should avoid describing a whole stockpile as a resource until representative testing and an actual use support the claim.
offer: Explore a characterisation and matching service through qualified mining, environmental and materials partners. Begin with authorised information and a safe representative sample. The first product may be a better decision record, a process-monitoring tool or a tested secondary input, rather than a new extraction operation.

firstPilot.title: A sample-to-specification assessment
steps: Define the stream, ownership and sampling approach with the responsible operator and qualified advisers.
Obtain the proposed customer's acceptance criteria before selecting a processing method.
Commission appropriate characterisation and compare variability across representative samples.
Model processing, water, energy, transport and residual handling as one complete system.
firstPilot.deliverable: A reviewed characterisation report and a decision on whether a specific reuse pathway warrants further work.

evidence.known: The planning title is Mining Process Byproducts. No deposit, recovery yield, treatment process or commercial resource estimate is supplied.
evidence.unknown: Whether a useful component can be recovered consistently without unacceptable cost or residual impacts.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Representative composition, accepted product yield, total inputs and the properties of material left behind.

businessModel: Characterisation, monitoring or specialist process services may precede any recovery venture. Commercial claims require evidence specific to the stream.
leadershipDecision: Count the residual stream and long-term obligations in the business case, rather than focusing only on the valuable fraction.
risks: Selective samples can exaggerate value.
Recovery can concentrate unwanted constituents elsewhere.
Transport, water and energy may dominate the outcome.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Can women in the mining and materials workforce shape the characterisation question and identify overlooked practical constraints?
Who would own the knowledge and share the value if a mining byproduct gained a useful new market?

title: Water Pollution
oneLine: Turn a water-quality concern into a clear observation programme and a practical response pathway.
need: A community may notice discoloured water, litter or changes after rainfall without knowing what measurements would explain the problem. Different pollutants require different methods and responsible authorities. The enterprise opportunity is to connect a precise question, credible sampling and understandable reporting, not to promise a universal purifier.
offer: Explore a monitoring or coordination service with qualified water professionals and a willing local group. Start with one catchment question and make sampling methods, units, locations and uncertainty clear. Any treatment proposal should be a separate project tested against the actual contaminant and intended water use.

firstPilot.title: One water question, a sound evidence trail
steps: Define the concern and intended decision with the people affected and an appropriate water professional.
Agree sampling locations, timing, handling and analysis with a qualified laboratory.
Collect authorised observations and present them with contextual rainfall or activity information where relevant.
Review the results with the responsible people and identify a proportionate next measurement or action.
firstPilot.deliverable: A traceable observation record, plain-language findings and a next-step brief.

evidence.known: The catalogue names water pollution as a theme. It does not establish a contaminant, source attribution or effective treatment.
evidence.unknown: What is causing the observed concern and whether available measurements are sufficient to distinguish possible explanations.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Sample quality, repeatability, coverage of the question and usefulness to the responsible decision maker.

businessModel: Monitoring coordination, reporting or instrument support may be useful services. Treatment sales require specific demonstrated performance.
leadershipDecision: Choose how results will be shared so communities can understand uncertainty and challenge an interpretation.
risks: One sample may be unrepresentative.
Correlation can be mistaken for a pollution source.
A low-cost sensor may not measure the contaminant of concern.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Which water-use question matters to local women, and can they choose what is sampled and explained?
Would women receive understandable results and a real route to influence the responsible organisation's response?

title: Computer E-Waste
oneLine: Keep computers useful for longer through repair, trustworthy data handling and responsible recovery.
need: Discarded computers may contain usable parts, private information and materials requiring appropriate handling. A local enterprise can create value by distinguishing repairable equipment from material recovery. People also need affordable support and confidence that a refurbished device will work for their actual tasks.
offer: Explore a repair and refurbishment service with a clear intake process, authorised data handling and tested product specifications. Pair experienced technicians with paid learners and make tools, benches and training usable for varied bodies and experience levels. Leadership should include decisions about warranties, pricing, customer support and ownership of the enterprise.
users: Schools or community groups where authorised

firstPilot.title: A traceable refurbishment batch
steps: Accept a small authorised batch with ownership and data-handling instructions recorded before inspection.
Classify devices for repair, parts or a qualified recycling route and document the reason.
Refurbish suitable devices using a repeatable test checklist and an agreed support period.
Ask recipients to use the devices for defined everyday tasks and track failures and support time.
firstPilot.deliverable: A tested refurbished batch, intake-to-destination record and realistic service pricing.

evidence.known: Computer E-Waste is an original theme. No collection authority, certified recycling operation or guaranteed data-erasure capability is claimed.
evidence.unknown: Whether recoverable value and customer demand cover diagnosis, repair, data handling and support.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Devices returned to useful service, repeat failures, technician time and verified downstream destinations.

businessModel: Repair fees, refurbished sales and organisational service contracts may combine. Include warranty and support costs rather than pricing only the repair bench time.
leadershipDecision: Set a quality and data-handling standard the team can demonstrate, and decide when a device should not be resold.
risks: Private data may remain without a verified process.
Uncertain parts history can cause repeat failures.
Unusable material can accumulate without a confirmed destination.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Can women with different technical backgrounds access tools, paid learning and progression into repair leadership?
Who controls customer data and product-quality decisions, and are women included in the enterprise's ownership?

title: DNA RNA Embryo Ark
oneLine: Explore biological preservation as an institution-led stewardship and continuity question.
need: The DNA RNA Embryo Ark title combines very different materials, purposes and ethical responsibilities. A preservation concept must first state whose material is involved, why it would be held, who may decide its use and what continuing care requires. It must not treat people, embryos or cultural relationships as interchangeable items in a technical archive.
offer: Begin with a non-biological information model for an existing authorised collection or a fictional conservation scenario. Document provenance, permissions, storage dependencies, access decisions and continuity arrangements. Any work involving human genetic material or embryos belongs with appropriately authorised institutions and specialist ethical and legal review, separate from this planning exercise.

firstPilot.title: A fictional collection continuity exercise
steps: Choose a clearly bounded collection purpose and use fictional records or authorised non-sensitive metadata.
Map ownership, consent, permitted uses, storage dependencies and the people responsible for decisions.
Run scenarios involving a funding interruption, record error or disputed access request.
Have qualified collection and ethics specialists review the model and identify missing obligations.
firstPilot.deliverable: A stewardship data model, continuity plan and list of questions requiring institutional resolution.

evidence.known: The catalogue provides an ark ambition, not a biological collection, preservation protocol or consent framework.
evidence.unknown: What materials and purpose are intended, whether preservation is technically appropriate and who would legitimately govern it.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Traceability of each fictional record and the ability to resolve continuity and access scenarios.

businessModel: Collection information management or continuity planning may be a practical service. Biological preservation requires a distinct institutional programme.
leadershipDecision: Define legitimate stewardship and participant rights before discussing storage scale or a civilisation-resilience claim.
risks: Different biological materials require different treatment.
Consent and future use can be misunderstood.
Long-term preservation creates obligations beyond a startup's life.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Who would have authority over any women's biological material, its future use and the choice to restrict or withdraw access?
Can women affected by a collection shape its purpose and governance without pressure to contribute personal material?

title: Drilling, Tunnelling, Lateral Mining
oneLine: Develop useful excavation tools by selecting one measurable problem in a qualified engineering setting.
need: Drilling, tunnelling and lateral mining involve different ground conditions, machinery and operating responsibilities. The city-scale vision should not obscure a more practical enterprise in inspection, monitoring, tool wear or planning. A useful founder asks an experienced operator where information or equipment currently fails them.
offer: Explore a digital planning tool or non-hazardous component test with a qualified civil or mining partner. Focus on one operation and document the conditions it represents. Women in technical trades, engineering and project management should have direct authority over design choices, including equipment fit, shift patterns and access to skilled progression.

firstPilot.title: One operator-defined excavation problem
steps: Interview an experienced operator about a specific recurring limitation such as inspection access or tool-condition records.
Define the ground, geometry and operating assumptions with qualified engineers.
Build a simulation, data tool or safe bench test that isolates the selected problem.
Review results against the current method and state what remains untested in real ground.
firstPilot.deliverable: A validated problem brief, controlled test result and next-stage engineering specification.

evidence.known: The archive lists the field but does not establish a machine, ground model, excavation authority or construction project.
evidence.unknown: Whether the proposed tool improves reliability or decision quality under the intended operating conditions.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Error, detection quality, operator effort or component wear against a specified reference task.

resources: Authorised records or controlled test rig
businessModel: Specialist software, inspection or component services may offer a route into the sector before developing major machinery.
leadershipDecision: Choose a narrow capability with a buyer and a credible test, and include worker experience in the success criteria.
risks: Bench conditions may omit real ground variability.
A data tool can be used beyond its validated scope.
Maintenance and recovery may dominate operating cost.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Would women operators and maintainers be able to use the proposed controls, access points and equipment comfortably?
Can women in technical trades influence the test plan and gain decision-making roles beyond administrative support?

title: Minimum, Ideal, Maximum Limits
oneLine: Define the operating limits of a proposed habitat in terms people and engineers can both examine.
need: Minimum, ideal and maximum are meaningless without saying what is being measured and for whom. A habitat could meet a narrow engineering minimum while leaving people crowded, tired or unable to participate. The venture should distinguish survival constraints, acceptable everyday conditions and the aspirations residents choose for themselves.
offer: Develop a requirements and scenario tool for one shared environment, beginning with ordinary facilities or a non-habitable research model. Include space, temperature, noise, privacy, access, workload and service continuity, with each limit linked to evidence or a clearly stated participant preference. Do not collapse diverse people into one ideal user.

firstPilot.title: A shared-environment requirements workshop
steps: Choose one environment and invite users with varied bodies, ages, caring roles and access needs.
Define each quantity or experience being discussed and separate professional requirements from preferences.
Compare a minimum-service, comfortable and expanded scenario using explicit assumptions.
Ask participants to identify unacceptable trade-offs and the decisions they want authority over.
firstPilot.deliverable: A traceable requirements matrix, scenario comparison and list of unresolved disagreements.

evidence.known: The catalogue supplies a limits theme within subterranean cities. It does not provide validated thresholds for a specific habitat.
evidence.unknown: Which limits apply to the chosen environment and how people's needs interact under constrained resources.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Requirements with clear evidence, unresolved conflicts and user-rated acceptability of each scenario.

businessModel: Requirements facilitation and design-review services could help existing facilities and research programmes before any speculative habitat is built.
leadershipDecision: Decide who can reject an unacceptable condition and how minority needs remain visible when averages look satisfactory.
risks: Averages can conceal serious exclusion.
A survival threshold can be misrepresented as a desirable standard.
Unverified numbers can acquire false authority through a dashboard.
equalityQuestions: What do women want from their environment beyond merely coping with it?
Which needs are being hidden by an average body, household or working day?
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.

title: Eternal Maintenance
oneLine: Make long-term maintenance visible, funded and possible for the people who must do it.
need: The phrase Eternal Maintenance captures a real concern but cannot promise permanence. Buildings and equipment need inspection, spare parts, skills, records and replacement. A resilient system also needs a plan for changing suppliers, ageing staff and interrupted funding. These ordinary responsibilities deserve as much design attention as the original installation.
offer: Explore a maintenance-planning service for one existing asset or a defined prototype. Connect each important function to its inspection, access, failure response and replacement path. A women-led enterprise could combine technical coordination, training and records while creating routes from hands-on maintenance into management and ownership.

firstPilot.title: One asset through a failure and replacement cycle
steps: Choose an asset and gather authorised manuals, service records and user reports.
Map critical components, access needs, spare availability and the consequences of losing each function.
Rehearse a failure response and a component replacement without disrupting a live essential service.
Prepare a funded maintenance schedule and handover record another competent team can understand.
firstPilot.deliverable: A maintainability review, service schedule and continuity handover pack.

evidence.known: The archive names eternal maintenance as a design ambition. No system can be declared indefinitely reliable from this concept.
evidence.unknown: Whether the selected asset can be maintained affordably through staff, supplier and component changes.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Time to identify a fault, access a component, obtain support and restore the defined service.

businessModel: Recurring asset-support and maintenance coordination may be viable where responsibility and response standards are clearly agreed.
leadershipDecision: Protect maintenance funding and worker knowledge from being sacrificed to a cheaper purchase price or a more impressive launch.
risks: A supplier may stop supporting a component.
Records can become stale after modifications.
Maintenance labour may be omitted from the budget.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Whose maintenance work is currently invisible, and how would women doing it gain paid time, training and authority?
Can women maintainers change a design that is difficult to reach, repair or support in a regional location?

title: Ultra Fast Transport
oneLine: Judge fast transport by complete journeys, access and dependable operation rather than headline speed.
need: Ultra Fast Transport is a broad ambition whose value depends on where people start, where they need to go and what happens at each transfer. A fast vehicle can still produce a slow or inaccessible journey. Women travelling with children, equipment, mobility aids or after dark may identify priorities that a speed-focused model misses.
offer: Develop a journey-planning and service-comparison tool for one real mobility need. Compare timetable changes, better transfers, existing vehicles and speculative high-speed options using the same door-to-door measure. The first enterprise could coordinate services or improve access while researchers investigate more ambitious infrastructure separately.

firstPilot.title: One journey from door to door
steps: Recruit varied users to describe a recurring journey, including waiting, transfers, luggage and care responsibilities.
Map current options and measure the complete journey under representative conditions.
Compare practical service changes with any proposed fast-transport architecture using explicit assumptions.
Test an information or coordination improvement with willing operators and user feedback.
firstPilot.deliverable: A journey evidence map, service comparison and a practical improvement brief.

evidence.known: The catalogue's fast-transport ambition does not identify a validated vehicle, route, operating authority or construction programme.
evidence.unknown: Which part of the journey creates the greatest burden and whether speed is the most useful improvement.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Door-to-door time, missed connections, access barriers, reliability and user-defined comfort.

businessModel: Journey planning, operator coordination or access assessment may support an early service. New transport infrastructure has its own engineering and demand case.
leadershipDecision: Choose whose journey defines success and ensure quieter or less frequent users influence the design.
risks: Average travel time can hide difficult transfers.
A model may ignore disrupted services.
A speed claim can distract from affordability and access.
equalityQuestions: What would make this journey usable for women with different bodies, work hours and caring responsibilities?
Would faster travel give people more control over time, or simply extend expected working hours?
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.

title: On Demand Production
oneLine: Make a useful product when it is needed, with quality, repair and local skills built into the service.
need: On-demand production can reduce waiting or excess stock, but it also requires reliable design files, materials, equipment, quality checks and a customer who needs the result. A small workshop should not promise to manufacture anything. The strongest starting point is a repeatable product family or repair component it can make well.
offer: Explore a local making service for a non-critical item such as a storage fitting, display component or workshop aid. Compare producing locally with buying and holding stock. Women new to technical work should have access to suitable tools, paid learning and genuine design and business decisions, not only administrative tasks.

firstPilot.title: One product from request to accepted delivery
steps: Choose a non-critical product with a willing customer and a measurable acceptance specification.
Confirm design rights, materials, equipment capability and the quality checks required.
Produce a small authorised trial through a suitable workshop and record all setup, finishing and inspection time.
Ask the customer to test fit and use, then compare the complete service with existing supply.
firstPilot.deliverable: A tested product, repeatable job record and a realistic quotation method.

evidence.known: The archive proposes on-demand production. It does not establish a universal manufacturing system or certified production capability.
evidence.unknown: Which product family creates enough local value to cover setup, quality control and support.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Accepted first-pass output, turnaround time, rework, material use and complete job cost.

resources: Clear design rights and quality checks
businessModel: A per-job making and repair service can be tested with actual orders. Price design and setup work transparently rather than hiding it in unpaid labour.
leadershipDecision: Set the boundary of what the workshop can reliably make and create a referral path for critical or specialist work.
risks: A cheap prototype may hide expensive finishing.
Unclear design rights can prevent reuse.
Poor quality control can produce parts that fit visually but fail in use.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Can women with varied experience use the tools and design files, with paid time to learn the production process?
Who owns the design, sets the price and decides how the value of a locally made part is shared?

title: Eternal Human Life Support
oneLine: Study resilient life-support services without claiming that an engineered habitat can sustain people forever.
need: Eternal Human Life Support combines water, air, food, power, waste, health, maintenance and social life. The word eternal is an ambition, not a measurable engineering guarantee. A useful programme begins with one service, a stated duration and a clear account of outside inputs and human responsibilities.
offer: Develop a systems model for a limited shelter, remote facility or research habitat, using qualified professionals and no live human-dependence trial. Track consumption, replenishment, failure recovery and the work required to maintain the environment. Include privacy, bodily needs, care, culture and the ability to leave, rather than treating people only as resource loads.

firstPilot.title: A service-continuity tabletop model
steps: Define a limited environment, occupancy scenario and time period with qualified advisers.
Map inputs, outputs, reserves and dependencies for one essential service before linking other systems.
Run scenarios for equipment failure, delayed supplies and unavailable staff using conservative assumptions.
Invite diverse prospective users to identify missing daily-life requirements and unacceptable conditions.
firstPilot.deliverable: A reviewed dependency model, failure exercise and next-component test brief.

evidence.known: The source expresses a long-term life-support ambition. No indefinitely self-sustaining habitat or complete closed-loop system is demonstrated.
evidence.unknown: Which external inputs remain essential and whether the proposed environment can support a dignified life over the stated period.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Service continuity, unaccounted inputs, recovery time and user-defined acceptability in the model.

businessModel: Continuity analysis or a validated component could become a service for existing remote facilities. A complete habitat needs a separate integrated engineering programme.
leadershipDecision: Make the limits, exit options and continuing human obligations explicit before describing the system as resilient.
risks: Failures can propagate between essential services.
Models may omit maintenance labour and replacement parts.
Survival metrics can hide an unacceptable quality of life.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: What would women want from a long-duration habitat beyond survival, including privacy, care, relationships and a meaningful way to leave?
Whose daily labour keeps the life-support model working, and do those women have authority over its design and limits?

title: Resurface & Expansion Planning
oneLine: Plan how a settlement could adapt, return to the surface or expand without trapping people in the original design.
need: A resilient settlement needs options when conditions change. Resurfacing and expansion raise questions about land, ecology, access, livelihoods and who decides the next phase. The concept should include the possibility that people prefer to leave or change the plan rather than assuming continuous growth is always desirable.
offer: Create a scenario-planning tool for an explicitly hypothetical settlement or an existing facility considering adaptation. Compare phased expansion, service upgrades, relocation and restoration using the same human and environmental criteria. The enterprise could provide participatory planning and dependency analysis without making site or construction claims.

firstPilot.title: Three futures for one hypothetical place
steps: Define the starting conditions and clearly mark which details are fictional or supported by records.
Co-design three different futures with participants, including a non-expansion option.
Map service, land, ecological and governance dependencies for each pathway.
Identify reversible first actions, decision triggers and the evidence needed before committing to major works.
firstPilot.deliverable: A scenario atlas, decision-trigger table and a staged research or planning brief.

evidence.known: The archive links resurfacing and expansion to subterranean cities. No site, settlement or agreed development programme is established.
evidence.unknown: Which future conditions would justify expansion, return to the surface, relocation or a different form of adaptation.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Unresolved dependencies, reversibility of early actions and participant understanding of the trade-offs.

businessModel: Scenario workshops and adaptation-planning services can be tested with existing organisations before a speculative settlement is involved.
leadershipDecision: Protect future residents' ability to revise the original plan and choose their own environment.
risks: Growth assumptions can exclude restoration or exit.
A compelling map can imply land rights that do not exist.
Long time horizons can hide unfunded obligations.
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.
equalityQuestions: Can women residents choose restoration, relocation or a smaller future rather than having expansion decided for them?
What housing, care and livelihood continuity would women need during a transition back to the surface or another place?

title: Gamification of Governance
oneLine: Make civic participation engaging while keeping real decisions accountable to the people affected.
need: Game elements can make learning and participation inviting, but points are not a substitute for voice, power or fair process. A governance tool should begin with a real decision and ask who is absent, what access they need and how participation changes the outcome. Women with little spare time should not need to compete for attention.
offer: Develop a cooperative participation experience around the planning document's Scan, Design, Simulate, Do, Share sequence. Recognise learning, care and follow-through without turning recognition into money or investment rights. The tool would help a willing group understand options, contribute in different ways and see what happened to its input.

firstPilot.title: A shared-space decision people can follow
steps: Choose a small decision with a willing group and state who holds authority to act.
Offer accessible ways to observe the need, propose options and try a simple simulation.
Run one agreed activity and record contribution, learning and observed results with participant permission.
Review whose input changed the decision and whether recognition encouraged cooperation or competition.
firstPilot.deliverable: A tested participation flow, transparent decision record and revised recognition rules.

evidence.known: The current plan defines C-Hour as recognition of verified community time with no economic equivalent, and supplies the participation sequence.
evidence.unknown: Which forms of recognition help this group participate without creating pressure, exclusion or performative scoring.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Participation breadth, actions completed, participant understanding of authority and useful changes made from feedback.

businessModel: Facilitation, educational tools or commissioned civic engagement may support a service. Keep financial accounts separate from contribution recognition.
leadershipDecision: Decide how people can influence the outcome without having the time, confidence or resources to earn the most visible recognition.
risks: Scores can reward easy-to-count activity over care.
A game can create the appearance of influence without real authority.
Public records may expose personal circumstances.
equalityQuestions: How can a woman with little spare time still shape the decision?
What forms of care or quiet contribution would a points system overlook?
sourceNote: Original concept from 500 Queens VC NEW Long, slide 16; current context from the September 2026 planning document. This expanded brief and pilot are proposed development, not evidence of an operating enterprise or confirmed partnership.

title: Olympic Scale Entertainment
oneLine: Use the ambition of major events to design entertainment that is accessible, locally useful and responsibly delivered.
need: Olympic Scale Entertainment is an ambition about reach and production, not a claim of Olympic affiliation or a confirmed programme. Large events depend on everyday work: rehearsal, transport, access, toilets, rest, staffing, rights and money. A useful enterprise can begin by solving one of those problems for a willing organiser.
offer: Explore an event-design or production service that combines a memorable audience experience with practical inclusion. Start with a small performance, installation or interactive programme, designed with women of different bodies, ages, languages and caring responsibilities. Test the service in a real venue before treating scale as a success measure.

firstPilot.title: A small event with major-event discipline
steps: Agree the purpose, audience and responsibilities with a willing host and creative team.
Design the audience journey from booking and arrival to seating, toilets, quiet space and departure.
Rehearse production, access support and disruption responses with the responsible professionals.
Run an appropriately authorised pilot and review the experience with audiences, artists and crew.
firstPilot.deliverable: A tested event format, audience-access findings and an operating brief for repetition.

evidence.known: The catalogue uses an Olympic-scale aspiration. No Olympic partnership, venue, date, artist or event permit is established.
evidence.unknown: Which experience audiences value enough to return to and what can scale without weakening access or working conditions.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Audience return interest, access barriers resolved, crew workload and delivery within the agreed resources.

businessModel: Production fees, commissioned experiences or ticketed programmes may be tested with a defined host and realistic costs. Rights and branding require clear agreements.
leadershipDecision: Choose what the event should contribute to its community and protect artist and crew conditions as attendance grows.
